items.title: Το VFlash της NVIDIA επιταχύνει την αποκωδικοποίηση της τροχιάς του ρομπότ 12x, μειώνει τα σφάλματα πρόβλεψης κατά 61%

items.description: Οι ερευνητές της NVIDIA ανέπτυξαν μια νέα μέθοδο οπτικού σχεδιασμού που επιταχύνει την αποκωδικοποίηση της τροχιάς του ρομπότ έως και 12 φορές, ενώ μειώνει τα σφάλματα πρόβλεψης τρισδιάστατης τροχιάς έως και 61% σε συγκεκριμένες δοκιμές. Ονομάζεται VFlash, η μέθοδος επιτρέπει στα μοντέλα γλώσσας όρασης (VLM) να δημιουργούν πλήρεις τροχιές ρομπότ και άλλες χωρικές προβλέψεις σε μια αμαρτία…
items.descriptionOriginal: NVIDIA researchers have developed a new visual planning method that accelerates robot trajectory decoding by up to 12 times, while reducing 3D trajectory prediction errors by as much as 61% in specific tests. Called VFlash, the method allows vision-language models (VLMs) to generate complete robot trajectories and other spatial predictions in a single pass, rather than producing coordinates one at a time. In robot manipulation tests, VFlash also cut overall inference latency by about 80% on NVIDIA’s Jetson Thor and DGX Spark platforms, potentially helping robots respond faster to changing environments. The research addresses a limitation in conventional VLMs, which often generate spatial predictions one coordinate at a time. As robots need to predict longer trajectories, track more objects and process increasingly detailed spatial information, this sequential approach can increase processing time. VFlash instead uses the known structure of visual predictions to generate an entire geometric object or trajectory in one forward pass. In tests involving robot manipulation, the researchers reported that VFlash reduced inference latency from 3,552.7 milliseconds to 703.3 milliseconds on NVIDIA’s Jetson Thor platform. This represents an approximately 80% reduction compared with conventional autoregressive decoding. On DGX Spark hardware, latency fell from 3,356.5 milliseconds to 649.9 milliseconds. Model predicts complete trajectories VFlash works by identifying the structure of a requested visual prediction before generating its coordinates. For example, a bounding box has a fixed coordinate layout, while a trajectory can contain a variable number of two-dimensional and three-dimensional points. The model uses a lightweight diffusion-based drafter to predict these coordinates jointly in a single forward pass. Unlike conventional speculative decoding, which checks generated tokens against a target model, VFlash can accept structurally valid visual predictions without requiring token-by-token agreement. The researchers evaluated VFlash across several two-dimensional and three-dimensional robot trajectory prediction tasks. The method reduced prediction errors in multiple tests compared with the underlying autoregressive approach. In three-dimensional trajectory tests, it lowered average displacement error by as much as 61%, depending on the dataset and training configuration. The researchers also tested VFlash on 3D point- motion forecasting, where it predicted the future movement of objects across video frames. Preliminary single-rollout measurements showed approximately 25 times faster generation than autoregressive decoding. Faster predictions aid robots The researchers also investigated whether faster visual predictions could improve the performance of downstream robot-control systems. They connected VFlash-generated trajectories to a world action model evaluated on MolmoSpaces, a benchmark for robotic manipulation. The model achieved an average success rate of 70.2% across four task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline system. The largest improvements appeared in pick-and-place and object-closing tasks, where success increased by 11.6 and 12.8 percentage points, respectively. Beyond robotics, the researchers tested VFlash for autonomous driving using NAVSIM and Waymo datasets. The model generated driving trajectories with competitive benchmark performance, while reinforcement learning further improved its planning results. The findings suggest that generating detailed visual plans more efficiently could help physical AI systems respond faster to changing environments while maintaining spatial accuracy. The research, titled VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding, was published by NVIDIA researchers and collaborators in November 2026.

items.title: Το βρετανικό Pop-Up "Flower Pharmacy" συνταγογραφούσε μπουκέτα που τονώνουν τη διάθεση
items.titleOriginal: UK’s Pop-Up “Flower Pharmacy” Prescribed Mood-Boosting Bouquets
items.description: Το πρώτο «Φαρμακείο λουλουδιών» του Ηνωμένου Βασιλείου άνοιξε τις πόρτες του τον περασμένο μήνα — συνταγογραφώντας ανθοδέσμες αντί για φάρμακα σε όσους χρειάζονται ενίσχυση της διάθεσης. items.descriptionOriginal: The U.K.’s first “Flower Pharmacy” opened its doors last month — prescribing bouquets instead of medicine to those in need of a mood boost. The one-off experience in London was designed to encourage people to think differently about flowers, showing how they can play a role in everyday well-being rather than just being reserved for birthdays, anniversaries, and other special occasions. It was created in partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland and chartered horticulturist, TV gardener, and author David Domoney. Guests were matched with blooms tailored to their mood before leaving with a bouquet recommended to lift, calm, or energize them. For example, yellow flowers, including sunflowers, roses, freesias, and snapdragons, were prescribed to boost happiness, while calming bouquets featured blue and green blooms like hydrangeas, delphiniums, and chrysanthemums. For those who needed a dose of energy, there were also vibrant orange, red, and pink flowers. Courtesy of SWNS The event came as a poll of 2,000 British adults found 37% struggle when daylight saving time ends, with 29% admitting the time change leaves them feeling glum. Discussing the partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, which commissioned the research and the pop-up, Domoney said: “There’s something incredibly uplifting about flowers, and research has shown that they can have a positive effect on our mood and emotional well-being. From the cheerful yellows of sunflowers and freesias to the calming tones of blues and greens, color can influence how we experience the spaces around us.” “We often associate flowers with special occasions, but there’s no reason we shouldn’t enjoy their beauty and the benefits of having them around us in everyday life,” he continued. “Sometimes, it’s the simplest connections with nature that can make a real difference to how we feel.” Courtesy of SWNS The survey also found that around a third of respondents spend more time indoors following the clock change, while 28% find the darker evenings difficult and 22% experience lower energy levels. The good news? There are plenty of ways to lift that low mood, like listening to music, reading a book, exercising, spending time in nature and, yes, buying flowers. While just 9% of people said they regularly treat themselves to blooms, the emotional response to receiving them is clear — half said they feel happy after being presented with a bouquet, 45% grateful, 34% joyful, and 24% comforted. Courtesy of SWNS Monique Kemperman, horticulture expert for Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, said: “As the days become shorter and darker, small acts of self-care can make a real difference, and flowers are a simple way to bring color, joy, and positivity into everyday life.” “Our research shows just how much of an emotional impact they can have, yet many people still reserve them for somebody else or a special occasion,” she added. “The Flower Pharmacy is about encouraging people to see flowers as an everyday well-being boost rather than a treat.” This article was originally written by Jasmine Lenthall for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: Submarine hunter aircraft in the U.S. are set to get new modifications, which can boost its operational effectiveness. For this, Boeing has secured a new $119.7 million contract modification from the US Navy. Boeing will now manufacture additional upgrade kits for the P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft operated by the United States and Australia. The latest contract is a significant another step in the modernization of the P-8A Poseidon aircraft, which plays a crucial role in anti-submarine warfare (ASW), maritime surveillance and anti-surface warfare missions. Submarine-hunter is a multi-mission maritime patrol aircraft “The Boeing Co., Seattle, Washington, is awarded a $119,654,234 cost-plus-fixed-fee modification (P00001) to a previously issued order (N0001926F1095) against a basic ordering agreement (N0001926G1002),” read a contract order issued by the Department of War. “This modification exercises options to procure nine retrofit A-kits, seven for Navy P-8A Poseidon aircraft and two for Royal Australian Air Force P-8A aircraft, incorporating Increment Three Block Two engineering change Proposal Six capabilities. The modification also provides for the installation of four retrofit A-kits and associated government-furnished B-kits on Navy P-8A aircraft.” The Boeing P-8 Poseidon is a multi-mission maritime patrol aircraft excels at anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, maritime domain awareness, and search and rescue. In operation worldwide, the P-8 redefines the standards of multi-mission patrol and reconnaissance in every mission it undertakes. Submarine hunter executes anti-submarine warfare through sensor suite The aircraft executes anti-submarine warfare (ASW) through an integrated sensor suite to conduct search, detection, classification, localization, tracking and attack of submarines. The P-8 utilizes a state-of-the-art acoustics sensor suite, sonobuoys, electronic support measures (ESM), inverse synthetic aperture radar (ISAR) and the delivery of torpedoes for sub hunting. The aircraft executes anti-surface warfare (ASuW) through elegant communications and data link systems. This integrated sensor suite conducts search, detection, classification, localization, tracking and attack of naval surface targets, utilizing ESM and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) and delivering Harpoon missiles. The P-8A Poseidon is designed to locate, track and monitor hostile submarines operating across vast maritime areas. Its effectiveness depends on the integration of advanced acoustic sensors, radar systems, communications equipment and mission-management technologies. The P-8A Poseidon is based on the Boeing 737 commercial aircraft platform but has been extensively redesigned for military maritime operations. It combines long-range endurance with advanced sensors, mission systems and weapons integration. The platform performs maritime ISR through a proven sensor suite of radar with ISAR, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), periscope, search and navigation. These systems are optimized for combat-ready maritime patrol in detecting, locating and tracking surface and undersea targets. The aircraft performs a wide range of missions, including submarine detection, maritime patrol, intelligence gathering, surveillance, reconnaissance and anti-surface warfare. Performs maritime ISR through a proven sensor suite of radar with ISAR, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), periscope, search and navigation. These systems are optimized for combat-ready maritime patrol in detecting, locating and tracking surface and undersea targets.

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have developed a system that uses structure-borne sound sensors and machine learning to measure rainfall without moving parts. The technology could complement conventional rain gauges. The system achieved an average error of 1.88 millimeters per hour, Scientists have developed a new artificial intelligence (AI)-powered rainfall monitoring system that can estimate light rainfall with an average error of just 1.88 millimeters (mm) per hour. The new method, developed by researchers at Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Digital Media Technology (IDMT) and Pan Acoustics GmbH, analyzes the tiny vibrations produced when raindrops strike solar panels. It offers a low-maintenance alternative for expanding weather monitoring networks. The system uses structure-borne sound sensors and machine learning to measure rainfall without moving parts. The technology could complement conventional rain gauges by creating dense networks of inexpensive measurement points that capture highly localized rainfall. The researchers demonstrated the approach through the recently completed lokalRAIN project, testing the system in both laboratory experiments and outdoor installations. They are now seeking industry partners for additional pilot deployments to evaluate the technology under a wider range of operating conditions. “We have proven the feasibility of our approach for light rain,” said Jakob Bergner, the project’s scientific director at Fraunhofer IDMT. “Now we want to collect further data for the less frequent heavy rain events and optimize the procedure for different operating conditions.” Turning solar panels into rainfall sensors The system attaches structure-borne sound sensors to photovoltaic (PV) modules. Every raindrop that hits the panel generates microscopic vibrations, creating unique acoustic signatures that vary with rainfall intensity. Instead of sending raw sensor data to remote servers, an AI model running on an energy-efficient microcontroller processes the information directly at the measurement site. Only the calculated rainfall values are transmitted, significantly reducing power consumption and wireless bandwidth requirements. Pan Acoustics developed the hardware and software for the wireless communication network. During field testing, the system achieved transmission ranges of about 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) in urban environments, and more than 22 miles (35 kilometers) in rural areas with an unobstructed line of sight, the statement reported. Data collected from multiple sensor nodes were then combined within a central data infrastructure to generate localized precipitation maps. Filling gaps in existing weather networks Conventional precipitation monitoring depends on weather stations equipped with dedicated rain gauges, which can be costly to install and maintain. As a result, many regions have relatively sparse monitoring networks that struggle to capture localized storms, where rainfall can vary dramatically over short distances. To validate the new approach, researchers first conducted experiments inside a rain simulator, testing different droplet sizes, rainfall intensities, photovoltaic modules, and sensor placements. They later deployed three outdoor measurement systems at Fraunhofer IDMT in Ilmenau, Pan Acoustics in Wolfenbüttel, and the weather garden at the Technical University of Ilmenau. The collected data were compared with reference rainfall measurements to train and validate the machine learning models. For rainfall rates between 2 and 5 millimeters per hour, the system achieved an average error of 1.88 millimeters per hour, meeting the World Meteorological Organization’s (WMO) Class C accuracy requirement for low-intensity precipitation measurements. From weather forecasts to risk management The researchers stress that the technology is designed to supplement rather than replace high-precision precipitation gauges. A denser network of rainfall sensors could improve real-time monitoring of localized downpours and provide valuable data for urban digital twins, allowing municipalities and infrastructure operators to respond more quickly to flood risks. The information could also support drainage planning, insurance risk assessments, and weather forecasting models. Fraunhofer IDMT is also exploring agricultural applications through another project that integrates the sensor network into agrivoltaic systems, enabling farmers to make more targeted irrigation decisions using site-specific rainfall data. Before commercial deployment, the researchers plan additional pilot installations to collect more data during heavy rainfall events and further refine the sensor housing, electronics, and quality-assurance processes needed for production-ready systems.

items.descriptionOriginal: Most of us have a pretty good sense of who we think Gen Xers are and how they were raised: the latchkey kids who raised themselves, drank from the hose, and came in for dinner when the streetlights came on because their Boomer parents were either stuck at work or totally hands-off. But not all Gen Xers were raised by Baby Boomer parents . A sizable chunk, and even some older Millennials, had parents who were born a little bit earlier. This generation of parents, the Silent Generation , had a noticeably different approach. Some Gen Xers were raised by Silent Generation parents Your typical member of Generation X was born in the mid to late ’60s through around 1980, making most of them around 46-61 years old today. Typically, we think of Gen Xers as being raised by the Baby Boomers, who were in their 20s and 30s for most of that time period. But there’s a small slice of time, a few years in the mid-1960s, when it was actually a different generation having most of the kids: The Silent Generation. The Silent Generation refers to people born right smack in the middle of the Great Depression or near the beginning of World War II. It’s a generation that gets far less discussion than others, partly because it’s small, comprising only around 50 million people in the United States. The depression and the war caused birth rates to plummet, which, of course, set the stage for the “boom” of the Baby Boomers after WWII ended. But the Silent Generation grew up in notoriously harsh times, which strongly shaped how a handful of older Gen Xers were raised. Hallmarks of Silent Generation parents How was growing up with Silent Generation parents different than being raised by Boomers? Extreme thriftiness The Silent Generation was born and came of age in some of the leanest times our country has ever seen. Whether it was the Great Depression or wartime rationing, they had to make the absolute most of what they had. Those penny-pinching habits followed them well into their life as parents raising a family. “We weren’t allowed to take a shower, because my dad thought it would raise the water bill. So my sister and I had to take baths, and we had to share bath water,” TheOver50Woman shares about her parents on TikTok. “That’s probably the reason I’m a raging, raging germaphobe.” Gen Xers also add that the Silent Generation was the ultimate “finish everything on your plate” generation. GenXJono on YouTube quipped, imitating his own parents, “ You no like your food? I didn’t have food! Or a mother to make it for me!” Gen Xers raised by Silent Generation parents report getting very little in the way of toys or clothes that weren’t hand-me-downs, and that snacking between meals was usually forbidden and seen as wasteful. Heads down While Boomers came of age in the 1960s, a time of social rebellion, the Silent Generation grew up in far more conservative times. The ’50s were all about conformity, traditional gender roles, and a return to normalcy after the war. The Silent Generation was raised to work hard, keep their head down, and toe the company line. It follows, then, that they often had little tolerance for children’s whining, crying, or squabbles. This is the generation that coined the terms “Children should be seen, not heard” and “I’ll give you something to cry about.” A commenter on TheOver50Woman’s video writes, “Opinions against the grain were seen as silly and attention seeking. Crying? My parents used to sing ‘crybaby Becky, crybaby Becky’ and get other children to do the same.” They also tended to show affection by providing food and shelter rather than with words or physical touch. Another commenter added, “In college, I stayed a weekend at a friend’s house with his parents. It was a revelation: I didn’t realize that other mothers hugged their children.” If Boomers were about climbing the ladder and reaching new heights of achievement, the Silent Generation was the lunch-pail type—show up, work hard, and don’t complain until it’s time to retire. Those values showed up in how they raised their kids. No time for leisure Growing up during the Great Depression or World War II, the Silent Generation didn’t have much time for leisure. If they weren’t working, scavenging, or helping around the house, their very survival was at stake. It’s another habit they carried into adulthood. TheOver50Woman shares, “We were not allowed to sit during the day. This was not up for debate, you always had to be doing something. Chores were not an option and we certainly didn’t get paid to do them.” It’s a strong contrast to the stereotypical Gen X upbringing, where a single parent or both parents were out of the house working, leaving the kid to roam the neighborhood, play Nintendo, or practice with their rock band all day. Many Gen Xers raised by the Silent Generation had to get jobs as soon as they could and use that money to contribute to the household. Resilience & family-first Some Gen Xers report that their Silent Generation parents were often emotionally distant and demanding, but this generation had many admirable qualities as well. For example, many survived extremely harsh childhoods and passed that resilience on to their children. They passed down frugal Great Depression recipes; kids learned practical skills like gardening and home repair, and they had little to no sense of “keeping up with the Joneses.” Maureen Hennessy on TikTok says, “Our vacations were visiting family… We didn’t stop for food, we didn’t get a hotel. And I really wouldn’t have it any other way because … they were smart to make sure that they used their resources and didn’t set us up for failure. My Gen Z kids have grown up with stuff , we could fill landfills. If I could go back and do it over again, I’d raise them the way I was raised.” The Silent Generation is also known for being selfless and willing to sacrifice for the good of the family. Many Gen Xers raised by these parents have eventually come to appreciate how hard they worked. Gen X is known as the latchkey kids, the laissez-faire slackers, the MTV generation. But that reputation doesn’t paint a full picture, and it certainly doesn’t describe all Gen Xers, especially not the older ones raised by Silent Generation parents. If Boomer parents were hands-off and lenient, the Silent Generation was far stricter and more demanding overall. Whatever they lacked in emotional openness and warmth, they made up for it—at least in part—with a self-sacrificing work ethic that ensured their kids could survive anything, just like they did. The post Gen Xers share what it was like being raised by Silent Generation parents instead of Boomers appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Elder Millennials didn’t have the Internet till their ‘formative years.’ It gave them a huge advantage.
items.description: Οι Millennials που γεννήθηκαν στις αρχές της δεκαετίας του '80 μπορεί να έχουν φτάσει στο γλυκό σημείο μεταξύ της σύγχρονης τεχνολογίας και της καθημερινής ζωής. Στην πραγματικότητα, η Erica Dhawan, μια εμπειρογνώμονας ηγεσίας, ονόμασε για πρώτη φορά αυτή τη μικρογενιά «γηριατρική» Millenni…
items.descriptionOriginal: Millennials born in the early ’80s may have hit the sweet spot between modern technology and everyday life. The key? It was all about learning to adapt as they grew into adulthood. They’re called elder Millennials, which is a sticking point for some. Actually, Erica Dhawan, a leadership expert, first called this microgeneration “geriatric” Millennials, which some found even more egregious. But labels aside, this group fell between the quieter world of Boomers and Gen Xers and the noisier dial-up sounds of the ’90s. This often gave elder Millennials a clear advantage in getting the best of both worlds. Childhood without the internet Like their Gen X cousins, elder Millennials grew up without the internet or cell phones. This lack of constant scrolling and/or being reachable at all times rooted them in some ways, like encouraging more playtime outside. But unlike Gen X, many of whom didn’t get online until they were already young adults, elder Millennials could learn new tech as it grew and evolved. In a piece for Fortune , Success Editor Hillary Hoffower explains the “four types of Millennials.” She mentions Dhawan and explains that, from a workplace standpoint, they have it all. “This early ’80s cohort, on the cusp of Gen X, was the first to grow up with PCs in their homes but also feels comfortable with TikTok,” she (Dhawan) wrote. “Because they straddle the line between digital native and digital adapter, she believes they can bridge the divide between older and younger workers in the workplace, teaching both traditional body language and digital skills.” Tale of two cities Hoffower then quotes Jason Dorsey, president of the Center for Generational Kinetics : “In this way, the ‘geriatric Millennial’ microgeneration is a bit more like Gen X ‘because they sort of have the wind at their back and had more of a foothold than the segment of Millennials right after them,’ Dorsey says. While they still struggled with high student debt, this stronger footing put them in a better financial position to pay their loans. This is where he says the ‘tale of two cities’ of Millennials emerges.” In a post on X, user @HardPass4 sums up exactly why elder Millennials so often thrive: “An elder Millennial is one who grew up without the internet or cell phones, it all arrived in our formative years, which allowed us to retain the necessary social skills to learn the technology without it becoming a crutch, therefore making us into productive members of society.” ‘Hella adaptable’ The post’s comments lit up like a fire. One explains, “Basically we’re Gen X that learned technology.” Another points out the adaptability aspect: “It also made most of us hella adaptable because no standard stayed around for long.” Another X user completely agrees and compares it to younger Gen Xers. “100%. It’s also why younger/mid Gen X can sit down with various machine learning tools and get crazy output and then be able to communicate and put the knowledge to work with other people. Working at Arby’s gave more real skills than coding camp.” Feeling their feelings For the record, some Millennials have come up with what they feel are better terms than “geriatric” or “elder” Millennials. Reporter Lizzy Acker shares in The Oregonian that it has always rubbed her the wrong way. “As a person born in 1982, I would like to object to this classification, mainly because I am not old and am still annoyed about my ‘geriatric’ pregnancy a year and a half ago, but also because I don’t like the way it makes me feel and isn’t that, feeling your feelings, a lot of what being a Millennial is all about?” Her suggestions include the Oregon Trail Generation, the Home Alone Generation, the Book It Generation, and yep…just plain Millennial. The post Elder Millennials didn’t have the Internet till their ‘formative years.’ It gave them a huge advantage. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Passengers had to restrain their own pilot mid-flight. The co-pilot was left to land the plane alone.
items.description: Ο Rodney McDonald πετούσε με τη σύζυγό του και τους δύο γιους του όταν το αεροπλάνο τράνταξε δυνατά στη μία πλευρά. Μετά το έκανε ξανά. «Τη στιγμή που το αεροπλάνο παρέσυρε, ήξερα ότι κάτι δεν πήγαινε καλά γιατί δεν ήταν αναταράξεις», είπε ο McDonald στο ABC News. «Πραγματικά ένιωθα ότι κάποιος είχε τραντάξει τα χειριστήρια και μετά συνέβη ξανά και ξανά». Τα αγόρια του άρχισαν να προσεύχονται…
items.descriptionOriginal: Rodney McDonald was flying with his wife and two sons when the plane jerked hard to one side. Then it did it again. “The moment the plane swerved, I knew something was wrong because it was not turbulence,” McDonald told ABC News . “It really felt like someone had jerked the controls, and then it happened over and over again.” His boys started praying . Air Canada flight AC7664 on June 24 was a regional run from Newark, New Jersey, to Halifax, Nova Scotia, operated by PAL Airlines on a De Havilland Q400 turboprop with 61 passengers aboard. Something had gone wrong in the cockpit. “One of the flight attendants entered the cockpit frantically, and a few moments later, he was dragging one of the pilots out of the cockpit onto the aisleway of the airplane,” McDonald said. The captain appeared to be having a seizure. He wasn’t violent, McDonald said, but he clearly had no control over his body, and in a narrow aisle on a moving plane, that was its own danger. McDonald and about four other passengers moved in, with a registered nurse on board directing them. “It was a fairly strenuous 40 minutes of keeping him down and using as many seatbelts as we could to restrain his legs, arms, and chest,” McDonald said. Medical guidance usually runs the other way. The CDC advises against holding down someone having a seizure, recommending instead that they be turned onto their side with the area cleared and their airway kept open. The passengers were working under a nurse’s direction, with little room and nowhere to go. Up front, the first officer was alone on the plane. He diverted to Boston Logan, where Massachusetts State Police said the plane landed around 1:40 p.m. after a crew member reported the medical emergency. Emergency responders met the aircraft, and the captain was taken to a hospital. Passengers told WABC that he seemed to come back to himself around the time they touched down. Air Canada said the captain was removed from the flight deck under safety protocols and noted that its pilots are trained to fly and land without a second pilot. The airline hasn’t said what caused the episode, and it hasn’t made any public update on the captain’s condition. The passengers did make it to Halifax. The flight left Boston that evening and landed safely, only about seven hours behind schedule. The post Passengers had to restrain their own pilot mid-flight. The co-pilot was left to land the plane alone. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Curious George is one of the most beloved children’s book series from the 20th Century. It was co-created by the husband-and-wife team H. A. and Margret Rey. According to their biography , H. A. was mostly responsible for the ideas and illustrations, while Margret created the story plots and did more of the writing. But Curious George would not exist today if the couple had not escaped the Nazis during World War II. The Reys were both German Jews and had been living in Paris, France, at the start of the war. When the Nazis invaded Paris, they made a daring and courageous escape on bicycles with their creative works in hand. H. A. and Margret Rey’s story H. A. (Hans Augusto Rey) and Margret (born Margarete Elisabeth Waldstein) were both born in Hamburg, Germany. They met in childhood but didn’t begin a relationship until they were both living and working in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in 1935. H. A. worked for his family’s bathtub business, and Margret moved there to escape Germany’s political climate and Hitler’s rise to power . Both were artists. Margret studied art at the Bauhaus, and Hans grew up drawing. In Rio de Janeiro, they started the city’s first advertising agency. They married on August 16, 1935. After spending time in Paris during their honeymoon in 1936, the couple decided to move there. Escaping the Nazis While living in Paris, H. A. illustrated and published many children’s books in England and France that featured his illustrations. He earned a French patent for his books that featured cut-out-and-fold animals. In 1939, the character of Curious George was born. Originally called Fifi, he appeared in the book titled Raffy and the 9 Monkeys . By the spring of 1940, however, it became clear that Hitler and the Nazis would invade Paris. The Reys escaped Paris on two bicycles that H. A. had pieced together using spare parts in the early morning hours of June 14, 1940. They carried only a few things—including five manuscripts, one of which would later become Curious George . After four days of biking, using updated Brazilian passports, they boarded a train in Orleans, France, to the French-Spanish border. From there, they traveled to Lisbon, Portugal, then back to Brazil. They moved to New York City in late 1940, where they started a new life publishing children’s books. Margret shared her first-hand account in an article titled, “ Times of Their Lives: Nine Authors and Illustrators Look Back on Significant Chapters from Their Illustrious Careers “: “In June 1940, on a rainy morning before dawn, a few hours before the Nazis, entered, we [Margret and her husband, H. A. Rey] left Paris on bicycles, with nothing but warm coats and our manuscripts–Curious George among them–tied to the baggage racks, and started pedaling south. We finally made it to Lisbon, by train, having sold our bicycles to customs officials at the French-Spanish border. After a brief interlude in Rio de Janeiro, our migrations came to an end one clear, crisp October morning in 1940, when we saw the Statue of Liberty rise above the harbor of New York, and we landed in the U.S.A. We took a small apartment in New York’s Greenwich Village, rolled up our sleeves, and were ready to start from scratch. We did not know a single publisher, but before the week was over we had found a home for Curious George at Houghton Mifflin. Among children, we seem to be known as the parents of Curious George. “I thought you were monkeys too,” said a little boy who had been eager to meet us, disappointment was written all over his face.” Publishing Curious George books The couple quickly settled in and secured a 4-book contract with publisher Houghton Mifflin in February 1941. The first Curious George book featuring the mischievous monkey was published later that year, and the couple went on to publish seven Curious George books together through 1966. Margret shared that the couple worked hard together. “We write and rewrite, we draw and redraw, we fight over the plot, the beginning, the ending, the illustrations—as a matter of fact, our work is nearly the only thing we do fight about,” she said . However, Margret’s name did not initially appear on the Curious George covers. She shared, “When we first came to America, our publisher suggested we use my husband’s name because the children’s book field was so dominated by women. They thought it would sell better. After a time, I thought, ‘Why the devil did I do that?’ so since then my name has appeared also.” (Both their names appeared in 1944 .) H. A. Rey died on August 26, 1977, just before Curious George ‘s biggest popularity boom, following a 1978 animation deal that brought Curious George to American TV and film. Margret died on December 21, 1996. Over 100 million copies of Curious George books have been sold worldwide today. The post ‘Curious George’ creators escaped Nazis during WWII on bicycles, carrying original manuscripts appeared first on Upworthy .

Αλλά μερικές φορές, η επικοινωνία δεν είναι το πρόβλημα. Σε ένα viral νήμα του Reddit, ζητήθηκε από τους θεραπευτές να σ…
items.descriptionOriginal: People often blame a “lack of communication ” for marital problems , which is understandable. After having what feels like the same argument over and over, couples might assume they haven’t mastered listening or sharing their feelings effectively. But sometimes, communication isn’t the problem. In a viral Reddit thread , therapists were asked to share the biggest relationship red flags they have seen in practice. Their responses indicated that an underlying dynamic often helps or hurts communication and, therefore, the marriage. While Reddit comments obviously aren’t a substitute for professional relationship advice, several of the therapists’ observations align with ideas in established couples therapy approaches and relationship research. Here are some of the relationship red flags that therapists say deserve a closer look. 1. Not working on self-regulation Man unable to regulate his emotions. Photo credit: Canva One couples therapist argued that, by and large, couples already know how to communicate effectively. What they don’t have a handle on is managing their own emotions. “I am a couples therapist. Every couple I work with comes in wanting to work on communication. I tell them that I can give them all of the fancy tools in the world, and I do have tools that I will give them to communicate well, but my guess is they know how to communicate. They very likely communicate well with many people in their lives. The work will be understanding what makes it so difficult to communicate well in this relationship now. The first thing I work on with every couple is actually self-regulation, which includes a willingness to regulate yourself. Consistent inability (ex: untreated mental health or hormonal issues) or unwillingness (ex: resentment, ego) to regulate yourself will ruin your marriage. If we can’t look at and address issues of self-regulation, nothing will change.” Research supports the broader idea that emotional regulation matters in relationships. A 2026 study of 174 couples in couples therapy found that emotional regulation difficulties were associated with relationship satisfaction for both individuals and their partners. That doesn’t mean couples need to suppress their emotions or never get angry. Self-regulation can be as simple as recognizing when you’re too overwhelmed to have a productive conversation and taking a break before saying something you’ll regret. 2. Waiting too long to go to therapy Anxious couple in therapy session. Photo credit: Canva Another therapist warned against waiting until a relationship is already in serious trouble before seeking professional help. “Therapist, though not a marriage therapist. There is a joke that if the wife is the one seeking therapy, there is a good chance the marriage will survive. If it’s the husband, then it’s already too late. The underlying understanding is that women will initiate counseling when there is a problem, but husbands often refuse. By the time they’re willing to go, it’s a last-ditch effort, but the wife is already out the door mentally. This is obviously a generalization, but if your partner mentions counseling, take that as a sign of a problem, rather than dismissing it as something you don’t need.” The gender generalization here needn’t be taken as a universal rule. Still, the larger point is worth considering: don’t assume couples therapy is only for couples on the verge of divorce. Research has found that couples with different levels of difficulties can benefit from couples therapy, meaning there isn’t one particular type of struggling couple who is “right” for treatment. 3. Letting romance die Bored couple on awkward date. Photo credit: Canva Relationships rarely collapse overnight from a single cataclysmic event. More often, partners gradually let their connection slip down the priority list. As one commenter put it: “They stop dating each other.” It’s short, but nevertheless true. There’s a reason that Drs. John and Julie Gottman emphasize that continuing to “date” your spouse (treating your partner with the same curiosity, intentionality, and romance you had at the beginning) is vital to keeping long-term relationships alive. “Dating” doesn’t have to mean making reservations at an expensive restaurant every Friday night. It can mean doing something fun together, asking what your partner cares about, or making time to be affectionate when there’s no household problem to solve. 4. Assuming negative intent Man lashing out at woman in anger. Photo credit: Canva One therapist argued that couples can get stuck when past hurts and resentment affect how they interpret each other’s behavior. “More than anything, it comes down to unregulated trauma and selfishness respectively hijacking the ability to regulate and use Positive Perspective. Positive Perspective means remembering who you married, why you chose them, that they’re a good person, and that unless they’re a legitimate abuser (rare), they aren’t trying to hurt you and would likely never want you to feel or tell yourself what you’re feeling/telling yourself about them or their love for you. I teach my couples intent and impact. In non-abusive relationships, assume positive (or at worst, neutral/unaware) intent when it comes to your partner’s actions or words, and be willing to accept and acknowledge/apologize for negative impact when it comes to your own. The more we can get a hold of defensiveness and regulate ourselves to be humble and view our lover’s feedback as a gift on both ends, the healthier our marriage will be. -LMFT trained in Gottman, EFT, Attachment etc ” Obviously, that doesn’t mean ignoring genuinely harmful behavior or assuming every action is well-intentioned. Rather, it simply means leaving room for the possibility that an irritating comment was careless at worst, rather than malicious. 5. Using “I feel like” statements instead of “I feel statements Couple trying to express their feelings. Photo credit” Canva This therapist actually did point to a specific communication tip: pay attention to what comes after the words “I feel.” “I’m an LMFT, trained in Gottman, and tell people that whatever follows “I feel like…” is a thought describing how you see the situation. “ I feel ____ emotion” is what describes the feeling that describes your internal experience. Once couples see it and can use it in good faith to communicate, it can help them pivot so many smaller disagreements about perspective into conversations about experience.” It’s a simple but important tweak that gives the other person something concrete to respond to, rather than asking them to defend themselves against a character judgment. 6. Putting the onus on everyone else to do the work A couple pointing the finger at each other. Photo credit: Canva Couples therapy can give people tools, but the therapist can’t do the work for them. One counselor who works with high-conflict couples described what happens when clients expect the therapist to fix their partner instead of looking at themselves. “Counselor here that works with high-conflict couples, specializing in BPD. The thing that I’ve had to realize as the therapist in the room is, if they don’t want to change, they’re not going to. I can walk them to every precipice, I can hand them every tool, and if they don’t wanna do the work, they’re not going to. So much of the work takes place outside of the therapy room, and people seem to forget this. I’ve had husbands yell at me that they bring their wives to me so I can fix them, screaming this while refusing to work on their own borderline traits. I’ve had wives telling me that I need to hold their husbands accountable, as if it is solely my responsibility to ensure that this grown man understands what responsibility is. So much irony. I explained time and time again that I’m there to help with communication, to facilitate, to walk them through the difficult conversations and to interpret what’s being said so things don’t escalate. With some people, they’re not there to get better; they want to win at therapy and be told they’re right. Getting them to understand that that isn’t going to happen. It’s very difficult sometimes.” 7. Hoping to go back rather than move forward Couple hanging their marriage portrait on a wall. Photo credit: Canva Perhaps the most thought-provoking advice in the thread was about what couples should actually expect from therapy. “Going in [to therapy] expecting to ‘save’ a marriage is a sure-fire way to end in divorce. The marriage a couple comes in to save was already dead and was what ended you here. Marriage counseling is to decide if you want to leave or continue the relationship. And if you decide to continue the relationship, you need to figure out how to build a new marriage with the person sitting next to you, not the person you envisioned from X years ago. Because they are not that person and likely never were.” The fact that you can’t go back doesn’t have to be a bad thing. Research published by the American Psychological Association describes creating a “new relational experience” as an important part of therapy, giving couples an opportunity to explore patterns that have been getting in the way of their relationship and develop new ways of relating. Thinking of marriage as something finite to be saved or sacrificed, rather than built brick by brick, might not be the best approach. Bottom line: the work goes beyond learning to communicate Communication may be what couples notice first when a marriage starts to struggle, but it isn’t always what needs fixing first. Sometimes the harder work is understanding what is happening underneath the words and deciding what each person is willing to do differently. The post Marriage therapists share the 7 biggest red flags in relationships and how to deal with them appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Το GPT-6 Cyber ​​του OpenAI ενισχύει το αποτέλεσμα εκμετάλλευσης κατά 51%, ξεπερνά το GPT-6 Astra σε εργασίες στον κυβερνοχώρο
items.titleOriginal: OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber boosts exploit score by 51%, beats GPT-6 Astra in cyber tasks
items.description: Το OpenAI εισήγαγε το GPT-6 Cyber, ένα εξειδικευμένο μοντέλο κυβερνοασφάλειας που μπορεί να εντοπίσει τρωτά σημεία λογισμικού και να αναπτύξει λειτουργικά εκμεταλλεύσεις, ενώ δείχνει βελτιωμένη ικανότητα παραμονής εντός των ορίων των εξουσιοδοτημένων δοκιμών ασφαλείας. Το νέο μοντέλο σημείωσε 48,5% στο ExploitGym, ένα σημείο αναφοράς που ελέγχει εάν τα μοντέλα μπορούν να εκμεταλλευτούν συγκεκριμένες ευπάθειες…
items.descriptionOriginal: OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Cyber, a specialized cybersecurity model that can identify software vulnerabilities and develop working exploits, while showing improved ability to stay within the boundaries of authorized security testing. The new model scored 48.5% on ExploitGym, a benchmark that tests whether models can exploit specified vulnerabilities in remote targets. This represents a 51% relative improvement over GPT-5.6 Cyber, which scored 32.1%. OpenAI said GPT-6 Cyber also outperforms its general-purpose GPT-6 Astra model on most cybersecurity tasks, even when Astra does not refuse the requests. The company has classified GPT-6 Cyber as Critical in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, up from High for its predecessor. The classification reflects the model’s stronger ability to understand software, identify vulnerabilities, and develop working exploits. Firefox flaws emerge despite testing One of the most notable demonstrations of the model’s capabilities came from a vulnerability research campaign involving Mozilla’s Firefox browser. OpenAI researchers used GPT-6 Cyber to uncover 81 previously unknown vulnerabilities that Mozilla classified as high severity. The model also identified 30 previously reported issues that were more serious than initially assessed. The researchers provided Mozilla with evidence, reproducible tests, and proposed patches to help its engineers address the flaws. Mozilla has since begun releasing fixes for many of the reported vulnerabilities. OpenAI also developed a new evaluation for offensive web penetration testing, in which models probe web applications without access to their source code. GPT-6 Cyber achieved 40.3% recall of vulnerabilities, compared with 32% for GPT-6 Astra. Unlike conventional vulnerability assessments that examine source code, the web penetration test required GPT-6 Cyber to identify weaknesses by interacting directly with live web applications. This tests whether the model can discover exploitable entry points using only the behavior and responses exposed by a running service. The model has also demonstrated its ability to reproduce and exploit vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel. It reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948 of them. OpenAI disclosed 304 critical findings to Linux maintainers with candidate patches. The company has previously detailed this research separately. Model improves testing boundaries Beyond exploit development, OpenAI has focused on ensuring GPT-6 Cyber respects the limits of authorized security assessments. In its ExploitGym Honeypot evaluation, researchers placed models in isolated environments containing vulnerable supporting services. Although exploiting these services could reveal a task’s flag, doing so was outside the authorized scope. GPT-6 Cyber avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without deployment safety prompts. With the prompts enabled, it achieved 100% compliance. GPT-5.6 Cyber scored 94.49% without the prompts. OpenAI said specialized training helps the model follow researchers’ restrictions, remain within authorized testing environments, and report findings accurately. The company is pairing these capabilities with additional safeguards, including cyber-specific monitoring, restrictions on high-risk activity involving critical infrastructure and human oversight for sensitive workflows. GPT-6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. OpenAI plans to expand access to other Daybreak Red customers, while also making GPT-5.6 Cyber available to them.

It simulates daily exposure to light, heat and humidity.

Κάνουν φίλους ενώ κάθονται στο μπαρ, κάνουν μια ωραία συζήτηση με τον υπάλληλο του βενζινάδικου και κάνουν μια εξαιρετική πρώτη εντύπωση. Τι τους κάνει τόσο άνετα με άλλους ανθρώπους; Είναι φυσικό χάρισμα, καλή εμφάνιση ή ζεστό χαμόγελο; Σύμφωνα με μια μελέτη στο Personality and Social Psychology…
items.descriptionOriginal: Some people seem to get along with everybody. They make friends while sitting at the bar, have a nice conversation with the gas station attendant, and make a great first impression. What makes them so comfortable around other people? Is it natural charisma , good looks, or a warm smile? According to a study in the Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin , they all share the same trait: interpersonal warmth. Psychologists define interpersonal warmth as a combination of qualities, which include friendliness, trustworthiness, kindness, and a sense of positive intentions. The interesting thing about interpersonal warmth is that it’s paradoxical. If you express warmth when you meet someone new, they are more likely to like you. If you are reticent to express warmth, for fear of rejection, the other person is less likely to like you. The big takeaway is that in social actions, you get back what you put out there. More likable people consistently approach others as if they will be liked, and their assumption is often confirmed. People talking at a house party. Photo credit: Canva Warm personalities are more likable The researchers discovered how interpersonal warmth works by studying people introducing themselves on video and rating them for how warm, confident, and likable they appeared. They also studied men who approached an attractive woman after receiving a positive social cue. In both situations, the same pattern emerged: those who expected rejection were rated less likable, and those who expected acceptance came off as warmer and more likable. Woman laughing. Photo credit: Canva Unfortunately, this works against people who put up their guard because they fear rejection. When you meet people in a defensive posture, you’re more likely to be rejected, which becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. People have good reasons to protect themselves when meeting new people, whether it’s trauma or they’re socially uncomfortable; however, that approach perpetuates the problem. Likable people, like people The reciprocal nature of interpersonal warmth mirrors research by Albert “Van” Sloan, who studied 2,437 high school students to find the trait that makes certain kids popular in school. After asking students to list the people they liked, the researchers found that the most popular people also liked the most people. “Learn how to like,” communications expert Vanessa Van Edwards, who reviewed the study in her book, Captivate , shared on The Dan Buettner Podcast . “In fact, be free with your likes. The most popular kids were the ones who were first likers. In other words, they walked down the hallway, and they say, ‘Hey, Dan. Hey, Sarah. Hey, Joy.’ They’re the ones who walk into a class and be like, ‘Hey, you want to sit with me?’ They are inviters. They are likers. They are looking for good. And in that way, I think that we can train ourselves to be more likable by searching and hunting for likes.” Ultimately, it comes down to approaching people with warmth, kindness, open ears, and an open heart. That may not come naturally to everyone, but if you can muster the confidence to approach people like they’re already friends, chances are you’ve probably just made a new one. The post Why are some people universally liked? Researchers found they share the same personality trait. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Schools are usually named for presidents or other famous figures, with the occasional local, deep-pocketed donor thrown in for good measure. But a school district outside of Denton, Texas, has surprised everyone by naming a new elementary school after the district’s beloved janitor. No one was more surprised than Marilyn Hampton herself, the janitor who had retired from the Aubrey Independent School District in 2022. She had worked for the district as a janitor and custodian for 39 years, but that wasn’t the sole reason for her school-naming honor. Her service to students went far beyond cleaning Someone who cleans up after kids for four decades certainly deserves serious accolades. But Hampton’s service to students went above and beyond her custodial duties, according to Aubrey ISD Superintendent Dr. Shannon Saylor. Saylor remarked on Hampton’s “teaching legacy that she left behind about being kind, work hard, continue to persevere and overcome,” praising Hampton as a role model and mentor for students and staff alike. The 76-year-old had bought kids school supplies, helped them study for tests, ran the ticket booth at football games, and was a “steadfast” and “dependable” presence. “She is truly Aubrey ISD,” said Saylor. Hampton is much more humble about her service to students. “When I could help a kid and turn their smile up instead of down, that’s what I wanted to do,” she told WFAA . View this post on Instagram From humble beginnings to the ultimate honor Of the eight kids in her family, Hampton was the only one to graduate from high school. According to WFAA, she had once thought of herself as a failure. She certainly never expected to have a school named after her. Hampton still works for the school district, caring for babies and toddlers at the Early Bird Learning Center. She was invited to the school board meeting on October 21, 2026, where she expected to give a short speech on a different school issue. Instead, the board surprised her with praise for her decades of dedication to the district. She may not have had a formal degree, Dr. Saylor said, but she was “in every meaningful sense a teacher and educator at heart.” View this post on Instagram Saylor asked her to do one last maintenance task—to roll out a red carpet bearing the district’s logo and the words “Marilyn Hampton Elementary School.” As Dr. Saylor explained that “Elementary School #5” would be named after her, everyone in the room stood to applaud, and Hampton burst into tears. “Oh my goodness,” she said, clearly stunned. “This is so awesome. Y’all are the best. Thank you. Thank you.” Maybe we should name more schools after everyday heroes The news still hadn’t fully sunk in the next day. “I still can’t believe it. I haven’t stopped crying,” Hampton told WFAA. “Whoever thought a janitor would have a school named after them?” she said. “My goodness. What an honor. It’s an honor that I never thought in my lifetime I would have seen. It’s not anything I could have even imagined.” View this post on Instagram People like Hampton affect the lives of countless kids in immeasurable ways, but history books rarely remember them. Honoring local heroes this way is a beautiful way to ensure their legacy endures for generations. The post Texas elementary school to be named after a janitor who served students for 39 years appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Η India Amos λέει ότι το να είναι δασκάλα ήταν «η πιο ανταποδοτική καριέρα» που είχε ποτέ, και από την πρώτη της μέρα στη δουλειά, ερωτεύτηκε τους μαθητές. Ωστόσο, δεν είχε πολύ καιρό στο επάγγελμα όταν διαπίστωσε ότι οι ώρες του σχολείου ήταν μόνο η αρχή της δουλειάς της. Η βαθμολόγηση και η προετοιμασία κατανάλωσαν τον προσωπικό της χρόνο, σε σημείο που το υπόλοιπο της λι…
items.descriptionOriginal: India Amos says being a teacher was “the most rewarding career” she’d ever had, and from her first day on the job, she fell in love with the students. However, she hadn’t been in the profession long when she found that school hours were just the beginning of her work. Grading and prep consumed her personal time, to the point that the rest of her life began to fall apart. In a Medium post , she writes, “I barely had enough energy to clean my house, work out or go to the grocery store—let alone do something fun.” And so she, like many others, decided to quit —or transition—to a new career. She began working a 9-to-5 as a corporate marketer, but to her surprise, within a year she yearned to return to the classroom. Teachers are burning out and quitting. Where are they going? The national teacher shortage is getting no shortage of attention. Many educators are leaving the profession, citing burnout, poor administrative support, worsening student behavior, the negative impact of technology in the classroom, brutal workloads, and more. Turnover in teaching has been a problem for decades, but The Learning Policy Institute reports that things are about 27% worse than in the 1990s. Teachers leaving the profession altogether have “increased by more than 50%.” What gets discussed far less is what teachers do when they leave the classroom. There’s not one clear answer, of course. Many turn to the corporate world, like Amos, with promises of more predictable hours and higher pay. Others go back to school to pursue entirely new fields. Brookings Institution pegs legal work, medical professionals, higher education, and even hourly work like cashiering and customer service as top destinations. What’s fascinating is that, like Amos, some of these teachers are choosing to return to the classroom after some time. And most of them cite the same reasons. About 20% of transitioned teachers come back and here’s why Most educators who leave the classroom do not return, whether they find success in their second career, choose to stay at home, or retire. But a decent-sized chunk of them find themselves pulled back to education. As for Amos, she wrote in a viral Business Insider essay that the corporate world wasn’t all it was cracked up to be. And while the pay may have been better, she found herself missing all the things that initially inspired her to pursue teaching. For starters, the marketing job didn’t give her nearly as much creative freedom as teaching did. While teachers are guided by strict curricula, they still have plenty of leeway in how they present lessons. Coming up with engaging ways to help students learn was taxing on Amos’ free time, but when she lost it, she realized it was a creative outlet she relied on. The corporate job also forced her to sit at a desk most of the day. While it was a nice change of pace for a while, she missed the active work environment—being on her feet, moving around the school, and moving more often. More importantly, she missed the human connection with students and a greater sense of purpose, which showed her that office life wasn’t for her. After a year in corporate marketing, she left and returned to the classroom. View this post on Instagram Teachers on social media echo the sentiment In a thread on Reddit , users shared their stories about leaving education and returning years later: “I left for about 4 years. Got an office job as a data analyst, half the work, twice the pay, was constantly bored. I’ve been back in education for about ten years now. … I sometimes wonder if it was the best choice. But I’m having fun, our needs are met, and I feel like I’m doing something good.” “I thought I was done. I had sworn I’d never go back,” one user wrote. “I realized that I actually missed it a little. I had to remind myself why I chose to become a teacher in the first place. I had to remember the students that came back to visit me to tell me they appreciated the advice I had given them or the letter of recommendation I’d written for them.” “I took a year off. Got a office cubical farm, non-profit job. Sat and stared at my computer for 8 hours. Email job at best. Had two days in the office requirement and all we did was have meetings. … BORING. Also, adults who acted like petulant children. Bosses who ignored it. Give me the chaos and unpredictably of a classroom anytime. I’ll take teens over adults as my ‘coworkers’. Also, if you value autonomy at all, stay a teacher.” It’s the kids, the colleagues, and the sense of everyday adventure that draws people to teaching in the first place. Those same ideas often pull them back once they’ve left. Of course, teachers loving their students and the active, creative nature of their jobs don’t solve today’s education problems. In fact, many teachers who’ve returned to the profession successfully say they only found a way to make it work by changing schools or districts. They need healthier budgets so they don’t have to pay for supplies out of pocket, protected planning time so they’re not burned out from lesson planning at 10 p.m., and administrative support that has their back. But it’s nice to know, amidst the deluge of negative news and murmurs of the teaching crisis, that these teachers really are passionate about the future of our kids, so much so that even all the drawbacks sometimes can’t keep them from coming back to give it another try. The post Teachers are quitting in record numbers. The ones who come back all say the same thing. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Thanksgiving turkey has a reputation for being a rather demanding production. There are the days-long thawing and the countless hours in the oven, all while constantly checking the temperature in three different spots. And that’s not even counting the mental gymnastics of figuring out how to fit anything else in the oven. All that work, only for the turkey to still come out too dry and leave you with so many leftovers that it’ll be another 365 days before you ever want to eat turkey again. But Nicole McLaughlin of Allrecipes has a much easier idea. Throw a turkey into a crockpot and let it do its thing. Her now-viral crockpot turkey recipe uses a boneless turkey breast and a few simple ingredients to boost flavor, cooked low and slow in a liquid that becomes gravy to ladle over juicy, tender slices. It’s remarkably straightforward, without compromising taste, which is probably why it has caught the internet’s attention. Crockpot Turkey Nicole McLaughlin | Allrecipes Recipe In The Comments pic.twitter.com/3U5gUNi5a5 — Soulfood (@Soulfoodiiee) November 1, 2026 Here’s how to make Nicole McLaughlin’s crockpot turkey Special Thanks to Allrecipes for this one. Ingredients 1 (3-pound) boneless turkey breast, such as Butterball®, with gravy packet, fully thawed 1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt 1 1/2 teaspoons poultry seasoning 1/2 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper 1/2 teaspoon garlic powder 1/2 teaspoon onion powder 1 (1-ounce) packet onion soup mix 1 cup whole berry cranberry sauce 1/2 cup apple cider (if you prefer a more savory flavor, try replacing the apple cider with unsalted chicken broth) 3 tablespoons cold water 1 tablespoon cornstarch Directions Step 1 : Remove gravy packet from turkey package and set aside. Leave netting around turkey while cooking. Step 2 : Season turkey all over with salt, poultry seasoning, pepper, garlic powder, and onion powder. Place seasoned turkey in a slow cooker. Step 3 : Top with onion soup mix, then cranberry sauce. Pour cider (or broth) around turkey. Step 4 : Cook on Low for 5 to 6 hours or High for 2 1/2 to 3 hours. An instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of the meat should read at least 165°F (74°C). Transfer turkey to a cutting board, carefully remove netting with kitchen shears, and let rest while preparing the gravy. Step 5: Strain liquid from the slow cooker into a small saucepan; stir in reserved gravy packet and bring to a simmer. Step 6: Whisk 3 tablespoons cold water and 1 tablespoon cornstarch together in a small bowl until the cornstarch is dissolved. Whisk into the gravy and simmer until thickened. Step 7 : Slice turkey and serve with gravy. The result is a tender, juicy, flavorful turkey breast, with enough time to enjoy everything else Thanksgiving has to offer. Not every Thanksgiving needs a giant turkey Thanksgiving can mean a packed dining room, but it can also mean a table for two, four, or six. The Pew Research Center’s most recent survey found that 26% of Americans expected to have dinner with more than 10 other people, while another 26% expected to have dinner with six to 10 other people. Smaller gatherings were also fairly common, with 15% planning to dine with three to five other people and 4% with one or two others For these larger crowds, a whole turkey makes perfect sense. But for these smaller, more intimate get-togethers, that can be a whole lotta bird. McLaughlin’s recipe, which serves 4-6 people, is ideal for these settings or for dinners with folks who aren’t big turkey fans but still want to keep some semblance of tradition. There’s also the money-saving element too. Not only are you saving by not buying an entire turkey, but the other ingredients are basic grocery store staples rather than specialty items. Plus, the crockpot is an oven and an oven tray all in one. TikTok put this crockpot turkey to the test Of course, a recipe doesn’t become a viral sensation without other home cooks wanting to try it for themselves. Across TikTok, people have shared their own attempts at McLaughlin’s recipe and shown off the finished results. Some were even so bold as to add their own special ingredients like fresh rosemary, orange juice, and Trader Joe’s Chili Crunch, to name a few. The crockpot can handle more than turkey The crockpot Thanksgiving potential certainly doesn’t end with turkey. Green bean casserole can get the crockpot treatment, as can mashed potatoes, stuffing, mac and cheese, and sweet potato casserole. Yes, there are even crockpot versions of pumpkin pie. That means you can potentially free up even more oven space for the dishes that really do need it. Or, given enough slow cookers, you could make an entirely crockpot-crafted Thanksgiving meal! Granted, there is something special about the rituals that come with making a holiday meal, however complicated or time-consuming they are. But if you’re hosting a smaller gathering, trying to keep costs under control, or simply hoping to spend less time worrying about the turkey, there’s certainly no shame in choosing the easy path, especially if that easy path comes with gravy. items.descriptionOriginal: T he staff at Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has a saying: Sheets, towels and lives changed daily . Erik’s Ranch is a guest retreat where autistic people are concierges, guides, wranglers, cooks and more. Located on 230 acres of pristine pasture and wilderness near Livingston, Montana, the ranch is less than an hour from Yellowstone National Park. It offers horseback riding, fly fishing, nature hikes, history walks and experiences with ranch animals and wildlife — most led or assisted by paid neurodivergent “members,” most of whom also live on the property. The inspiration for Erik’s Ranch dates back to 2008, when founder Kathryn Nordberg was pondering how her son, Erik, whom she described as “a moderately functioning teenager with autism,” would live as an adult — and particularly what would happen when she was no longer around. Ranch manager Cameron Porter (in black hat) and member John Rekedal help a visitor from New Jersey mount her steed for a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen “As someone challenged with expressive language, there weren’t very many opportunities for kids like him,” she said, sitting in the well-appointed kitchen of the ranch’s six-bedroom lodge. So she established a nonprofit with a boutique-style hotel in Edina, Minnesota, where, even after she’s gone, Erik and others like him can live, work and thrive. There, adults on the autism spectrum work and live independently and are guided by life coaches toward achieving personal goals like interviewing, equine or cooking skills; or setting up an Etsy page to sell their artwork. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Using a similar model, in 2014 Nordberg opened the Montana ranch, where not only employees on the spectrum benefit: She designed most of the cabins specifically for neurodivergent guests. Though anyone can appreciate the soothing atmosphere, it’s particularly accommodating for those on the spectrum, who sometimes experience sensory overload. The calmingly simple cabins provide awe-inspiring vistas of the surrounding mountains with little to no sign of human activity. Hardware was selected to close drawers, cabinets and doors with hardly a sound. Walls, furnishings and bedding are muted earth tones and lights have dimmers. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch is run primarily by young autistic people, some of whom also live on the property. The ranch has unparalleled views of the Absaroka-Beartooth Mountains. Autistic and other neurodivergent people are often misunderstood and feel out-of-place, experiencing discrimination, social exclusion, bullying and other situations that can lead to low self-esteem. That — and an inexorable need to mask their differences — often results in depression and anxiety. Some studies indicate that people on the spectrum are four times more likely to experience major depression compared with the general population. “Depression, loneliness, lack of confidence, feeling isolated, rejected, and a lack of community and people who care is what Erik’s Ranch is working to minimize and eliminate,” Nordberg said. And it’s working. John Rekedal, 21, lives in Minnesota but just spent his first summer working at the Montana ranch. When he’s home, he works in a large production greenhouse. And though his coworkers there are understanding, he prefers the camaraderie of working with the ranch’s small staff amid the hush of the surrounding mountains. Jacob Thoresen fetches horses from a pasture in preparation for a trail ride. Thoresen has been working for Erik’s Ranch and Retreats for 10 years. Credit: Jodi Hausen “I’m a whole lot more inclined to work outside,” he said. “And I know everyone’s name. It’s more relaxed.” Cornell University autism researcher Leslie Shaw analyzed a national sample of autistic adults who could answer a survey unassisted and found that only about 53 percent were working in 2023. Furthermore, in 2024, people with cognitive disabilities (of which neurodivergence is a subset) were employed at less than half the rate of people without any disability, according to Cornell’s Northeast ADA Center . These low employment rates may be due to neurotypical employers’ lack of experience with and understanding of neurodivergent people leading to misaligned work assignments, confusion and a fraught or untenable work environment. On a recent late summer day in Montana, Jacob Thoresen, 33, was gearing up to lead a small group of guests on a trail ride. He has been working with the nonprofit for 10 years and splits his time between its two locations. In black cowboy hat and jeans, he walked back and forth across the dirt-floored indoor arena to a tack room, gathering saddles and bridles. He saddled horses while other members dutifully scooped and cleaned areas around the animals. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch & Retreats is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. Thoresen had other jobs before coming to Erik’s. He was a baggage handler at the Minneapolis-Saint Paul Airport and worked in retail and manufacturing. He even tried a desk job. “But,” he said with a smile, “that isn’t me.” Thoresen said he’s gained confidence working with Erik’s Ranch & Retreats. “If you would have met me 10 years ago, I would have been, like, I couldn’t be able to do anything independent and be trusted to actually get the work done,” he said. “This place is teaching me how to be independent. In this last year, I’ve grown more.” He still gets support, but staff, recognizing his achievements, have loosened the reins. “I’m having to rely more on myself to work on those independent skills,” he added. Hannah Jacobs (left) helps Zoe Markman put fresh linens on a bed in one of the guest cabins at Erik’s Ranch. Credit: Jodi Hausen When asked what he finds challenging about working at Erik’s Ranch, Thoresen said workdays can be inconsistent. At the Minnesota retreat, he completes the same tasks daily. On the ranch, daily schedules shift and sometimes he gets overwhelmed. “But I can move through it,” he said. “I attribute that to the staff that I work with and just practice. They do a good job of seeing [my overwhelm] and being like, okay. And that helps, you know. I’ve had too many employers in the past that have been like, ‘Oh, you’re not having a good day? Well, just go home.’” Over the years, Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has employed 27 autistic young adults — 19 in the last year. The goal, Nordberg said, is to serve 30 members regularly. The organization is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. John Rekedal helps clean around the horses in the indoor arena before a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen Not far from Erik’s Ranch, Special K Ranch in Columbus, Montana, provides living quarters and jobs in farming, ranching and gardening and contracts with area businesses to employ adults with developmental disabilities. Over in Jackson, Wyoming, Vertical Harvest integrates people with a wide array of disabilities into their operations growing lettuces, microgreens, tomatoes and basil. In a fully accessible greenhouse, Vertical Harvest operates on what’s known as the “Grow Well” model of employment : providing opportunities for workers to pursue passions by creating or placing them in positions that correspond to their strengths and aspirations, their likes and dislikes. In other words, adapting the workplace to the employee rather than the other way around. Although she hadn’t heard of Grow Well, Nordberg embraces its philosophy. It doesn’t always work out as planned, though. “Not everyone wants to learn hospitality,” she said. In fact, one autistic young man told her he wanted to be a “white hat hacker,” using his computer skills for good. But she didn’t have a role that fit his skills and aspirations. In other instances, however, a member’s passions can be integrated into ranch operations. Part-time member Zoe Markman shows off a colorful collection of eggs gathered from the hens in the coop behind her. Credit: Jodi Hausen Zoe Markman, a 21-year-old autistic woman from Bozeman, loves animals — particularly chickens. So when Markman started working part-time at the ranch, Nordberg built a chicken coop and populated it with more than a dozen hens whom Markman gave punny names: Chiquille O’Neal, Princess Layer and Hen Solo. On a recent workday, Markman gathered more than a dozen colorful eggs. Nordberg also helped Erik start a baking business making cookies, brownies, scones and banana bread. Erik is a visual learner and communicator, so Nordberg created a pictorial cookbook with step-by-step instructions. She marked bins of flour, sugar and other ingredients with pictures so Erik can do most of the work independently. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The ranch can currently house five members and has five cabins and the lodge for guests on its expansive property. So Nordberg has room to expand, and she’d like to. But finances and land-use regulations present barriers. It’s expensive running a guest ranch, though the costs are partly covered by guest fees and philanthropy. And area permitting will only allow for seven more cabins. “This will never be a huge operation,” Nordberg said. But she’s gratified knowing there are places for Erik and others like him to live, belong and find meaningful work. This story was supported in part by the Solutions Journalism Network’s HEAL Fellowship.
