items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ ΑΙΣΙΟΔΟΞΟΥ Μια νέα θεραπεία που εγκρίθηκε από τον FDA για το PTSD ανέφερε ύφεση 68 τοις εκατό σε κλινικές δοκιμές. Τα εγκεκριμένα φάρμακα με την καλύτερη απόδοση για την πάθηση ξεπερνούν περίπου το 10,9%. Η θεραπεία, που ονομάζεται Μαγνητική e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), αναπτύχθηκε από την Wave Neuroscience με έδρα την Καλιφόρνια σε συνεργασία με…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A newly FDA-cleared treatment for PTSD reported 68 percent remission in clinical trials. The best-performing approved medications for the condition top out at around 10.9 percent. The treatment, called Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), was developed by California-based Wave Neuroscience in collaboration with researchers at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology. It pairs brain activity mapping with personalized magnetic stimulation. The clinical trial also reported a 52 percent reduction in PTSD symptoms overall. “Our FDA trial reported a 52 percent reduction in symptoms, so more than a four-fold increase in efficacy,” said Erik Won, D.O., Wave Neuroscience’s chief medical officer. “And more importantly, we saw 68 percent remission in our clinical trial. From a clinical care perspective, that’s really meaningful.” These results come from different studies, not a direct head-to-head comparison, but the gap is hard to ignore. How MeRT personalizes treatment The process starts with an electroencephalogram (EEG) that records each patient’s brain electrical activity. An AI-assisted algorithm uses that data to build a personalized stimulation plan. A coil placed against the scalp then delivers targeted magnetic pulses through transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a technique already FDA-cleared for treatment-resistant depression . Standard TMS follows a generalized protocol. MeRT adjusts based on what’s happening in each patient’s brain. Dr. Kenneth S. Ramos, a precision medicine researcher at Texas A&M Health who helped guide the study, put it this way: standard TMS covers the leak with a tarp; MeRT tries to find and replace the damaged shingles. Participants received five sessions per week over five to six weeks, but improvements appeared to persist after the sessions ended. The first FDA-cleared non-drug option for PTSD PTSD was formally recognized as a diagnosis in 1980 . Since then, treatment has relied on two FDA-approved medications, both SSRIs, and psychotherapy. A 2020 review found medication remission rates reached 10.9 percent at most. MeRT will be the first FDA-cleared non-medication treatment specifically for PTSD. Dr. Israel Liberzon, the study’s lead psychiatrist and a distinguished professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, explained what that means for patients. “Right now, the FDA has approved only two medications for PTSD,” he said. “This is the first time that in addition to the medication, we have a non-medication option. There is psychotherapy that people use for PTSD, but psychotherapies require a lot of effort. People must participate actively, and many drop out because it’s too anxiety-provoking. So now we have a unique alternative.” About six percent of Americans will experience PTSD during their lifetime, with higher rates among women and veterans . In the United States, approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day. “People living with PTSD have been left with trial-and-error treatment, medications and their side effects, and limited outcomes—even when treated by the most dedicated and experienced physicians,” Won said. “Wave’s FDA clearance signals a fundamentally different future: one in which PTSD can be objectively evaluated, precisely treated and meaningfully healed.” Wave Neuroscience and Texas A&M Health are working on insurance coverage to make the therapy more widely accessible. Won also believes MeRT could eventually be adapted for depression, anxiety, and other psychiatric conditions. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Chances are, you’ve got a tube of toothpaste in your bathroom right now. If it’s only going on your teeth, you’re leaving a surprisingly useful cleaning tool sitting on your bathroom counter. Joy Ramos , a professional cleaner and operations manager at Bear Bros Cleaning, has long used toothpaste for jobs well beyond the bathroom. Most white, non-gel toothpastes contain mild abrasive particles that work like ultra-fine sandpaper, polishing surfaces without scratching them. It turns out that property has a lot of household uses. One thing before you start: plain white, non-gel toothpaste is what you want. Gel formulas don’t have the same abrasive particles, and heavily whitening varieties can be too harsh on delicate surfaces. Always rinse thoroughly after using it, and when in doubt, test on a discreet spot first. For scratches and cloudy surfaces A light scratch on glass (a phone screen, a coffee table, a mirror) can often be buffed out with a small amount of toothpaste on a microfiber cloth. Work in gentle circles, then wipe clean. The abrasives smooth the area around the scratch rather than filling it, so it becomes much less visible. The same trick works on fogged car headlights. Rub toothpaste over the lens in small circular motions for a minute or two, then rinse and dry. Repeat if needed. Wood is another one. Water rings and minor scratches on countertops or floors respond well to a small amount applied with a soft cloth. Follow the grain, wipe off, and dry thoroughly. For metals and fixtures Hard water takes the shine out of faucets and handles over time. Toothpaste can bring it back on stainless steel and chrome, though there’s a catch: softer metals like copper and brass can be damaged by the abrasives, so skip those. Silver jewelry is a great candidate, too. Avoid polished metals and soft stones like opals, pearls, or turquoise. “Always use a gentle hand and test first,” Ramos says. For walls, shoes, and more Crayon on painted walls is a classic small-kid problem. Toothpaste can lift it, but the wall finish matters. “Due to the mild abrasives in the paste, flat or matte paint may sometimes fade or become damaged,” Ramos says. “And on darker or more delicate finishes, it could leave dull spots or streaks.” Glossy, light-colored paint holds up well. Toothpaste also works on white rubber soles and leather or canvas sneakers. Just keep it away from suede, mesh, or anything delicate; those materials can stain or break down. For a persistent stain on a toilet seat, apply a small amount with a cloth or toothbrush, scrub gently, let it sit a few minutes, and wipe clean. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: “Vibe coding,” is so last year. If you want to (try) to get on the same wavelength as teens and tweens, here’s another expression to add to your repertoire: Collins Dictionary has selected “mogging” as its 2026 word of the year. The slang term popular among Gen Z and Gen Alpha is defined as outperforming or outshining someone or something. Believed to be a shortened version of AMOG (alpha male of the group), the word traces back to bodybuilding culture around the 2010s. But it’s soared in popularity over the past year, with younger generations using it in a more playful way. Collins noted that experts found a 210% increase in usage of the “fast-growing slang word” in 2026, meriting the “word of the year” crown. So how do you use it? If your friend looks amazing in the selfie you just took, but your eyes are closed and hair is out of place — they’re mogging you. Or, to offer a more meta example, mogging is mogging the other words in the dictionary. Other words on the British dictionary’s shortlist include: Bixie : a haircut that’s shorter than a bob but longer than a pixie cut Fricy : a blend of fruity and spicy Friendslop : a low-budget, independently made video game designed to be played casually with friends Carspreading : the tendency of manufacturers to build cars that are longer, wider, and heavier Hydration break : a pause in a sporting contest to allow the contestants to drink fluids, especially in high heat Ghost job : a role advertised by an employer who has no intention of actually hiring anyone On Oct. 25, Dictionary.com announced its own word of the year: “Maxxing,” a shortened version of “maximizing” that can be used on its own or tacked on to the end of another word to describe the act of optimizing something. Derived from gamer lingo and in use for over a decade, the slang term broke through on TikTok in the 2020s. Its most famous usage is perhaps “looksmaxxing,” which refers to taking a person’s appearance to its full potential, but “sleepmaxxing,” “cozymaxxing,” and “booksmaxxing” have all joined the zeitgeist as well. “Really, anything in your life can get the maxxing treatment, if you do it wholeheartedly enough,” the online dictionary wrote in a blog post.

items.descriptionOriginal: P undits are describing last night as a romp for Democrats, a rebuke of Republicans, a blue tsunami, a rout in the red states. But underneath these headlines is a quieter, parallel story about voters choosing to abandon tribal allegiance and make decisions for themselves. For months, we’ve been hearing about the possibility of a blue wave — and then, in the same breath, the caveat: Is a wave even possible in today’s hyper-polarized America? And yet, in Texas, Florida, Kansas and beyond, the electorate refused to let party loyalty make their choice for them. Young, Latino and red-state voters moved, sometimes dramatically, in just two years. The composition of the two sides turned out to be less fixed than we imagined, with a meaningful number of voters willing to cast ballots across party lines when a candidate, issue or circumstance spoke to them. In Texas, where Democrats had historic wins, people of all parties have recently united to fight against a border wall through Big Bend National Park. Credit: Sam Karas Part of the story was turnout, said New York Times Chief Political Analyst Nate Cohn on The Daily . But, he added, “Many people who are registered as Republicans and voted for Donald Trump voted for the Democratic candidate.” This feels like a fitting conclusion to The Depolarization Project , our special series about how political polarization works and what we can do about it. The premise of that series was that depolarization isn’t about meeting in the middle. It’s about choosing to remain open and curious, rather than blindly clinging to arbitrary affiliations. In the end, many voters showed that their party label doesn’t have the final say. Data center opposition is proving to be a bipartisan, or even nonpartisan, issue across the U.S. Credit: Here Now / Shutterstock Wednesdays are normally “What We’re Reading” day here at Reasons to be Cheerful, so in that spirit, here’s a post-Election Day list of stories from our own depolarization series and from elsewhere around the web. We Hate to Break It to You, But Maybe We’re Not That Polarized – the New York Times A Wall Meant to Divide Is Uniting Left and Right in Texas – Reasons to be Cheerful Voters Vastly Underestimate the Open-Mindedness of Their Political Rivals – PsyPost The Door-to-Door Technique That Actually Changes Minds — Reasons to be Cheerful The post The Election That Transcended Tribalism appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Walkable Traveler: Discovering Philadelphia’s Greenest Neighborhoods on Foot Reading Time: 3 minutes The Walkable Traveler: Discovering Philadelphia’s Greenest Neighborhoods on Foot There’s a moment on most city breaks when you realise you’ve spent more time getting between places than actually enjoying them. You’ve waited for a taxi, sat in traffic, arrived somewhere only to discover it’s a ten-minute walk from where you were half an hour ago. It’s enough to make you wonder why you bothered with the car in the first place. Philadelphia is a city where I’d be inclined to leave it behind.Not everywhere is within walking distance, obviously, but a surprising amount of the central area is. The streets are laid out in a fairly straightforward grid, and there’s plenty to see without travelling particularly far. I’d probably start somewhere around Independence Hall, partly because it’s one of those places you feel you ought to visit, and partly because the surrounding streets are worth a look in their own right. From there, Reading Terminal Market isn’t too far away. I wouldn’t bother making elaborate lunch plans. With that many food stalls under one roof, you’re almost certain to find something you fancy, although deciding what to eat might take longer than expected. Afterward, you could head towards Rittenhouse Square. I rather like the idea of a park that doesn’t try too hard to be an attraction. Rittenhouse is simply a pleasant place to sit for a while, with trees, benches and people going about their day. Somebody’s reading a book. Somebody else is walking a dog that clearly has no intention of going home yet. Meanwhile, the surrounding streets are full of shops, restaurants and apartments. It feels like a proper part of the neighbourhood rather than somewhere created exclusively for visitors. Philadelphia has quite a few green spaces like that, although some are much smaller. Community gardens are particularly interesting. You might find one occupying what was once an empty lot, with vegetables growing in raised beds and a few chairs tucked into a corner. They aren’t necessarily places you’d travel across the city to visit. But coming across one while walking through a residential neighbourhood is rather lovely. And they tell you something about the people who live there. I’d also make time for South Philadelphia. East Passyunk Avenue has the sort of mixture I enjoy: independent shops, restaurants, cafés and ordinary residential streets just around the corner. You can wander without feeling you’re missing some major attraction because you haven’t followed a particular route. The nearby Italian Market area is worth including too, especially if you like looking around food shops. I’d probably end up buying something completely impractical to carry around for the rest of the afternoon. One thing I wouldn’t do is try to squeeze all of Philadelphia into a single walking itinerary. It’s a sizeable city, and there’s no prize for finishing your holiday with sore feet. SEPTA’s buses, trolleys and trains make it possible to cover longer distances without needing a car, which is useful if you want to explore beyond the central neighbourhoods. Where you stay can make the whole thing easier or considerably more annoying. I once heard somebody describe a hotel as being ‘only twenty minutes from everything’, which sounds wonderful until you realise they meant twenty minutes by car. For a trip focused on walking, I’d be looking at the actual streets around the accommodation. Is there somewhere nearby for breakfast? Can you reach a park without crossing several major roads? How far is the nearest transit stop? Those details matter more to me than whether the apartment has an especially impressive television. One of the most effective ways to practice eco-friendly travel is reducing reliance on automobiles during city visits. Philadelphia’s grid layout makes it one of the most pedestrian- and transit-friendly cities in North America, allowing visitors to walk from historic landmarks to local farmers’ markets with ease. Choosing a neighborhood rental situated near public transportation hubs and neighborhood parks allows travelers to experience authentic community life while keeping emissions low. Rather than juggling multiple booking platforms, smart travelers use independent meta-search portals to find well-located accommodations. Exploring Philadelphia vacation rentals via cozycozy gives travelers real-time access to available townhomes, lofts, and historic suites across every major rental portal, making it effortless to lock in a sustainable home base. I’d check the final booking details separately, particularly the exact location and any additional charges. Of course, there’s an environmental benefit to doing more of a city break on foot. Fewer car journeys generally mean fewer transport emissions , and using public transport for longer trips can help reduce your reliance on taxis or a hire car. But I wouldn’t spend the whole weekend thinking about my carbon footprint.I’d be thinking about where to get another coffee, whether there’s time to explore one more street and why I hadn’t left myself longer at the market. That’s probably what makes walking such a good way to experience Philadelphia. You get to see the famous buildings, but you also spend time in the places between them. The little gardens, the corner shops, the streets where nothing especially remarkable is happening.And sometimes those are the bits you remember most. The post The Walkable Traveler: Discovering Philadelphia’s Greenest Neighborhoods on Foot appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: "Acting is not a real job that pays. How will you survive with theatre?" For Lalit, whose father drove an auto-rickshaw and whose mother was a homemaker, it was a difficult question to answer. He loved theatre, but his family worried about how he would earn a living from it. But passion is stubborn that way. Even when today's questions go unanswered, it stays. Lalit kept training with theatre groups across Delhi , often paying out of pocket, until a poster near Mandi House, the city's theatre district, caught his eye. It was for Bargad, a fellowship offering free training and a monthly stipend. He instantly knew where he had to be. "What's the harm in trying, I thought to myself and am I glad I did?" he recalls with glee. In January 2025, he joined its first cohort of 14 fellows and on day one, co-founder Amba asked them to write down what they hoped to gain from the programme. "She asked us to re-visit it after six months," Lalit says. Lalit, whose father drove an auto-rickshaw, chose the stage over certainty, and a poster led him to Bargad. He had hoped that the programme would lead him to a "well-known drama school" and return with a qualification he could show his family. So he wrote, folded the paper and slipped it into a pocket. His family's question was still unanswered. But it was one Bargad had been built to confront. Who gets to tell their stories? Behind the fellowship was a larger question: who gets to pursue theatre when training costs money, time and the security of a regular income? For Amba, Co-Founder of Bargad and Academic Head of the Fellowship, the journey into this question began with her own experience of the performing arts. After training at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art and working in London for five years, she returned to India with a desire to build a theatre practice of her own. The question for her wasn't just one of who gets access to theatre training and professional opportunities, but whose stories, imaginations and artistic voices get valued in the first place. Co-founder Amba questions who gets through theatre's door, and who has historically been told it belongs to them. "I realised there is heavy gatekeeping in the performing arts, and how much of it is shaped by caste and privilege - an accident of birth," she says. "Who gets through the door? And historically, who has been told that the door belongs to them? Bargad is an attempt to question that gatekeeping," Amba says For Anirudh, Co-Founder of Bargad and Course Director of the Fellowship, the question became personal about 10 years ago, while working on a play about the Criminal Tribes Act. Until then, he says, his privileged background had blinded him to many inequalities. "I was born into a privileged caste and class with access to education and exposure, and I lived most of my life in a little bubble, blind to everything around me," he tells The Better India. "That play was my first honest encounter with the reality of caste and with Ambedkar's writings. It felt as if everything I had learnt and believed was a lie. The ground beneath me shifted." Anirudh's encounter with caste while staging a play on the Criminal Tribes Act changed how he saw everything. In 2025, this led to the founding of Bargad by Amba-Suhasini K Jhala and Anirudh Nair, with Sanyukta Saha, who runs the Agaaz Theatre Trust, and Shambhavi Singh, founder of Oddbird Theatre. Its first cohort began in January 2025. For Amba, widening access meant more than inviting new people into existing institutions. It meant changing the conditions that decide who can enter at all. Paying students to make theatre possible There on, Bargad's first answer was practical: make training free and pay the people undertaking it. Sanyukta Saha, who has spent years bringing theatre to Delhi's Nizamuddin Basti through Aagaaz, and Shambhavi Singh, co-founder of Oddbird Theatre, helped found Bargad in 2025. The first two cohorts received ₹10,000 a month and the third, which begins January 2027, will receive ₹15,000. Classes run from 4 pm to 8.30 pm, six days a week, allowing fellows to earn during the day. Many applicants are financial contributors in their families , and attending classes can mean giving up hours they would otherwise spend working. "For the fellows, the opportunity cost of taking time out to train in the arts is quite high," Anirudh says. "The guarantee of a stipend also helps convince their families." Before joining, Lalit had paid to learn theatre and sometimes depended on his siblings for money. The stipend gave him a measure of financial independence. "For the first time, I was being paid to do theatre," he says. "Initially I was in disbelief but I knew this would be a great opportunity to afford what I enjoyed the most. With the stipend, I did not have to ask my brother or sister for money, and I spent it on travel, books and personal necessities." Fellows train from 4 pm to 8.30 pm, six days a week, leaving daylight hours free to earn. He did not tell his parents when he was selected; only his brother knew. The question of what theatre could offer him remained unresolved, but for the first time, he had room to find out. Bargad also challenges the assumption that a lack of formal training means a lack of ability. Applications grew from around 75 in the first year to about 200 in the second. Candidates can apply in English or Hindi through written or video submissions. An independent online jury shortlists around 30 applicants for three rigorous in-person audition rounds, followed by a group audition testing their listening, collaboration, responsiveness to direction and ensemble skills. A second jury selects the final 14. "We keep the batch deliberately small so that each fellow receives sustained individual attention, close mentorship and the space to take risks, experiment and grow within a close-knit ensemble," explains Amba. The six-month curriculum covers voice, movement, acting, improvisation, writing and devising, with visiting practitioners from Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and Chennai. The emphasis is not only on learning techniques, but on finding ways to use them to make original work. A scene is never really finished Neel Chaudhuri, a devising teacher who has taught at Bargad since its inception, works with fellows to develop performances from prompts in the subject of 'Devicing' or as he puts it, "to learn to learn to look within and ideate on what story one would like to tell independently." In devising labs with faculty member Neel Chaudhuri, fellows return to short scenes every fortnight, learning that ideas grow through process, not perfection. In 'Divising Labs' held every other week, fellows build short scenes and return to them over time, watching how an idea changes with further work. "The idea is not that they have to make a perfect scene in two weeks, but that they should follow a process, learn how a story is conceptualised and all that goes into seeing it to fruition," he says. The distinction is important. Rather than treating the first version of a scene as a finished product, the process encourages fellows to revisit their choices, test different approaches and discover what the work might become. The focus is on developing an idea, not simply producing something quickly. That approach also opens up what can count as material for theatre. "A scene need not begin with an extraordinary event or a fully formed story. An everyday object, a remembered incident or a private discomfort can become a starting point. The work lies in examining the experience and finding a way to communicate it to an audience," Neel explains. Classes are conducted mainly in Hindi, and faculty are asked to work bilingually. "Fellows can ask questions and experiment without feeling that they must already know the conventions of theatre. And language is a big part of it," he says. When life becomes the story For Prerna Bisht, who joined the fellowship in 2026 after an unsuccessful application the previous year, that process began with food. Prerna Bisht turned childhood shame about hidden meals into a story of caste, secrecy and social pressure, and felt liberated. During a workshop led by Vamsi, an interdisciplinary theatre artist who explores the layered relationship between caste and food, fellows were asked to tell stories through what they ate. The prompt took Prerna back to her childhood in Haryana, where her family's non-vegetarian food was treated as something to conceal. "My father would shut every door and window while cooking so that nobody would know what we were eating," she says. "Once, a neighbour's child walked in, and we hurriedly hid our plates. For a long time, I was ashamed of my food and I often ate my school lunch hidden from everyone," Prerna recalls with a tinge of sorrow in her voice. The memory was about more than a meal. It captured how the fear of being judged could follow someone beyond the home, turning an ordinary part of one's life into a source of embarrassment. The workshop gave Prerna a way to revisit that experience and examine what it had meant to her. "At Bargad, food became a way into a story about social pressure, secrecy and the shame I had carried into school. I felt liberated," she says. Here, a first draft is only a beginning, and every scene is allowed to change This is one of the possibilities of devising: experiences that might otherwise remain private can be shaped into material for performance. The process does not erase what happened. It gives the person telling the story a way to look at it differently and decide what they want to share. Taking the story to the stage After any programme, the question that often arises in the minds of students is: "What next?" In theatre, that anxiety can be manifold with scarce opportunities, rising costs and inaccessibility. To solve this, the founders began Bargad ka Chabutra , a further six-month programme that alumni can apply to. It includes masterclasses on running workshops, fundraising and producing, among other supportive teaching. Students can also apply for one of two production grants of Rs. 1 lakh each. Lalit's cohort used one grant to expand a 15-minute scene about manual scavenging into Hawa Mahal , a full-length play. The group interviewed manual scavengers, whose experiences informed the production. Lalit then became a part of a larger production team and designed a set made from pipes and windows that also doubled as manholes. Hawa Mahal grew from a fifteen-minute scene into a full-length play on manual scavenging, with pipes doubling as manholes. Over seven months, the students developed the production, learning not only how to shape a story but also how to organise the work needed to bring it to an audience. For Lalit, that meant taking on responsibilities beyond acting and helping turn the group's research into a stage production. Finding space for the story Getting a play on stage presented another challenge. Auditoriums around Mandi House can cost ₹80,000 to ₹1 lakh a day, while affordable independent venues are limited and often booked well in advance. Hawa Mahal had six performances, including one at Ashoka University. For Lalit, the response after one performance made the work feel worthwhile. "After three shows, in a post-show meeting, the audience told us thank you for telling this story," he says. But taking a story from the classroom to an audience requires funding, rehearsal time and space. The ability to develop a production is of little use if there is nowhere affordable to stage it. "In theatre, it is impossible to work without space, both to build work and to show it to audiences," Neel says. Behind every performance lies unseen work: rehearsal, research, affordable space and funding. Bargad has tried to address this by building a network of spaces, people and resources that can help the fellows bridge the gap. Nikhil Mehta of Black Box Okhla has hosted the fellowship and its alumni programme. Other fellows have continued their work in different ways: a graduate from a village in Bihar received a Rs. 1 lakh grant to write a play, a fellow from the second cohort joined the National School of Drama, and another won a full scholarship to Drama School Mumbai. Keeping the door open Bargad's future depends on making these opportunities sustainable. Over two years, the programme has relied on around 20 to 25 individual donors, contributing between Rs. 5,000 and Rs. 5 lakh. With Delhi auditoriums costing up to ₹1 lakh a day, affordable stage space remains theatre's quiet barrier. Their support has helped keep it running, but relying on individual generosity makes long-term planning difficult. "Sustainability is not about finding more well-wishers every year," Amba says. "It is about finding long-term partners who understand that access cannot depend on annual generosity, so we can plan three, four, five years ahead." With more stable funding, she hopes to establish year-long courses in every metro, tour productions and offer larger bursaries. These ambitions would expand the opportunities available to performers who might otherwise struggle to enter the field. Giving theatre a future By the end of the fellowship, the qualification Lalit had once hoped for no longer mattered to him. With Bargad, performers like Lalit no longer need a certificate, only the confidence to stage their next play on their own terms. Photograph: (All images courtesy of: Akshita Doley and Santwana Saira John) "I had so much confidence by then that I did not need a tag," he says. "I can proudly say that I studied in Bargad's first batch. Now, I don't even know where that piece of paper I wrote on is," he laughs. His family's question, how will you survive with theatre, still has no single answer. But Lalit now asks it as someone who has put a play on stage, and who is no longer waiting for anyone's permission to make the next one.

items.descriptionOriginal: As more of the planet’s wild places are consumed by human sprawl, people are increasingly trying to protect wildlife by moving it out of harm’s way. While such relocations might help a construction project clear a regulatory hurdle, it’s often not doing much good for the wildlife, according to new research. Just 6% of amphibian and reptile relocations tied to development could be classified as successful, according to a review of such projects published recently in Conservation Biology . “Moving these species away from a construction site does not mean they will survive in their new home,” said Megan Winand , a University of British Columbia biologist and the lead author. The results offer a sobering look at the performance of this increasingly popular strategy, as development of everything from pipelines to parks clashes with species protections. And while the authors found evidence of ways to improve the performance of such transplant projects, the main takeaway is that it’s usually better to avoid destroying a wild animal’s home than moving the creature to a new one. “We need to prioritize protecting habitat and explore alternatives to current mitigation practices, which this review shows are often failing to achieve meaningful conservation outcomes,” said Winand. The scale of the issue is staggering. While there is no comprehensive count of how often critters are moved to make way for development, a separate 2026 study by many of the same authors found that in British Columbia alone, some 5.1 million amphibians and reptiles were moved just between 2019 and 2022. And the long-term fate of these animals was unknown, because the province didn’t require monitoring. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {height: auto;position: transplanted animals fared. They scanned the scientific literature for papers published between 2007 and 2023 that examined the fate of relocated amphibians and reptiles. All told, they looked at 256 case studies tracking everything from tortoises to alligators. Most of the research was concentrated in North America, Europe, Australia and New Zealand. Nearly 70% of the translocations were done for conservation purposes, such as releasing an animal into habitat that it once occupied. The rest were cases involving animals moved to get them out of the way of development. The researchers then graded a relocation’s performance based on a four-tiered system. The first level was when the original transplants were surviving. A project reached level two when those survivors were reproducing. The third level came when the population was growing. The final, highest level was if a paper showed evidence that the population had achieved longterm viability. Based on that grading system, development-related relocations earned an abysmal grade. Just 6% of the cases were shown to have reached the third or fourth benchmarks. Nearly half of them failed to hit even the first level – that the original population had survived the move. While conservation-related transplants performed more than three times better, that still meant they only reached the top two levels 19% of the time. They had total failures in nearly a quarter of cases. A closer look at the different studies revealed two factors that seemed to contribute to the greater success of the conservation transplants, the scientists found. Things turned out better in cases where people tried to removed threats to an animal in the place where it was being relocated. Higher scores were also linked to more long-term monitoring after the move. “Without adequate follow-up, we won’t know whether animals survive in their new location, reproduce or establish a population that can survive over time,” says Winand. “Relocated animals may also leave the release sites, encounter new threats or face difficult habitat conditions.” So there are things people can do to increase the odds that the transplants will endure. The high failure rate of even the conservation-related measures shouldn’t be taken as a sign of poor execution by the people involved, the authors note. Rather, it illustrates how hard it is to do such translocations, especially for long-lived species that reproduce slowly. It also reinforces a common insight into biodiversity-related work: It’s a lot easier to avoid breaking something in the first place than to try to fix damage later. items.descriptionOriginal: Most of us have a corner at home where plastic bottles, old newspapers and cardboard boxes collect until someone finally takes them out with the garbage. But what if that pile of waste could get you a plate of food instead? In Bhopal, homemaker Anjita Sabhlok is making that possible through the Kachra Caf , where people can exchange their household waste for food, drinks and everyday essentials. In just eight months, the caf has sent more than 45 tonnes of waste for recycling. The initiative, launched by homemaker Anjita Sabhlok through her NGO, Mannat, in collaboration with the Bhopal Municipal Corporation, is built around a simple thought: waste has value, and people may be more willing to manage it responsibly when they see that value for themselves. The question that sparked Kachra Caf For years, Anjita worked through Mannat to educate people about waste management and the environment. But awareness alone did not seem to be bringing about the change she wanted to see. "We're educating people, but are we really seeing a change?" she wondered. That question led her to think of a different approach. Instead of only asking people to dispose of their waste responsibly, why not give them a reason to collect and segregate it? What was once discarded as garbage is now helping residents earn a meal through the Kachra Caf . The idea became the Kachra Caf , where people bring plastic, paper and other household waste in exchange for food and everyday essentials. Each kilogram of waste has a fixed value, making the exchange straightforward for anyone who walks in with materials collected at home. From household waste to 45 tonnes recycled Getting people to bring their waste to the caf was not easy at first. Changing everyday habits takes time, especially when waste is usually seen as something to throw away rather than something worth collecting. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) Gradually, awareness grew. People began bringing their waste to the caf , learning to segregate different materials and helping ensure that the collected waste reached recycling channels. In just eight months, the caf sent more than 45 tonnes of waste for recycling. The number offers a measure of what can happen when an environmental message is paired with a practical action people can take in their daily lives. Instead of relying on awareness campaigns alone, the caf gives residents a direct way to participate. They can start with waste generated in their own homes and see it put to a different use. Could the idea work beyond Bhopal? For Anjita, the idea extends beyond one caf in Bhopal. She wants other cities to recognise that waste is not worthless and explore ways to encourage people to manage it better. In just eight months, the initiative has channelled more than 45 tonnes of household waste towards recycling. The Kachra Caf brings together two everyday needs: finding a responsible destination for household waste and making food or essentials accessible through an exchange. The next time a pile of plastic or paper builds up at home, it may be worth thinking twice before throwing it away . In Bhopal, that waste could be the very thing that gets you a meal.

items.descriptionOriginal: Diwali is a little more magical when the house is lit up, the smell of festive treats fills the air, and children run around excitedly, waiting for the evening celebrations to begin. For many little ones, the excitement also comes from the familiar crackle of firecrackers lighting up the sky. But for Surat-based mom Swati Jain, Diwali has become an opportunity to show her two young sons that the fun of crackers need not always come with smoke, noise, or fire. The family believes that the best Diwali memories are made together, through simple traditions that bring joy without adding to pollution. Instead of buying an entire box of firecrackers, Swati, a parenting content creator and mother to four-year-old Nirvaan and two-and-a-half-year-old Vayu, has introduced them to something rather different: homemade crackers made using ordinary wooden popsicle sticks. When woven together in a particular pattern and released, the sticks spring apart one after another, creating a surprisingly loud crackling sound. There is no gunpowder, flame or smoke involved. Just wooden sticks, a little bit of science and plenty of excitement. For the family, it has become more than just an alternative to conventional crackers. It is a festive activity that brings everyone together. When a trip to Delhi changed the way they celebrated Diwali Swati and her husband, who are both originally from Delhi, have experienced the city's pollution during the winter months for years. But a visit in December 2024, with their two young children, made them reconsider how they celebrated festivals. "We had lived with that air for years ourselves, but seeing my kids go through it was very different," she recalls. During the trip for a cousin's wedding, both boys began coughing, their eyes started burning, and the family had to take them to a doctor. The experience also made Swati think about the street animals that have to endure the pollution and are often frightened by the loud sounds of firecrackers. She is not against crackers altogether. The family still lights a few phuljhadis, anars and chakris together. However, she believes that moderation matters. Made using ordinary wooden popsicle sticks, these homemade crackers create a crackling sound without fire, gunpowder or smoke. "Crackers aren't the only reason Delhi's air gets so bad, but when the whole city bursts bombs and ladis late into the night, right when the air is already at its worst, it becomes dangerous," she says. Wanting to preserve the excitement of Diwali for her children without adding to the pollution, she began exploring alternatives. That is when she discovered the idea of popsicle-stick crackers. Meet the crackers that go crackle without the smoke The idea is simple: ordinary wooden ice cream sticks are woven together in a zig-zag pattern, with each stick slightly bent and locked against the next. When the finished chain is placed on the floor and released, the sticks spring apart in quick succession, creating a crackling sound similar to a ladi. Explaining the science behind it, Swati says that each stick stores a little energy when it is bent. Releasing the first stick sets off a chain reaction, much like dominoes falling one after another. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Nivu and Vayu || Mom of 2 Toddler Boys (@nivuandvayu) "The crackle is just the wood hitting the floor and each other. There's no gunpowder, no fire, no smoke, and no chemicals. Just wood, and the energy from our own hands," she explains. For Diwali, the family uses around 80 wooden sticks to make one cracker. A pack of 200 to 300 sticks costs approximately Rs 300 at a stationery or craft store and is enough to make about three. The process takes around 10 minutes once the sticks are ready. Swati and the boys first paint them using child-safe colours and leave them to dry for an hour. She then weaves the sticks together, keeping one hand on the chain to prevent it from releasing prematurely. The weaving requires adult supervision because the sticks remain under tension. Once the chain is ready, the family places it on the floor, moves their faces away and lets it go. The same sticks can be collected and reused throughout the festive season. From painting sticks to bursting crackers, everyone has a role What makes the activity especially enjoyable for Swati is how involved her children have become. When they first tried it during Diwali 2025, Nirvaan was three and Vayu was around one and a half. The boys were too young to have a clear idea of conventional firecrackers, so the homemade version became their introduction to the fun of bursting crackers. "The first time I let one go, Nirvaan burst out laughing and wanted it again and again. Vayu just sat there clapping," she says. They repeated the activity seven or eight times that day and continued making the crackers every few days until Diwali. The boys get involved by painting the wooden sticks with child-safe colours before their mother weaves them together. This year, the excitement has returned. Nirvaan enjoys painting the sticks, while Vayu helps by handing them over and placing a few during the process. Swati says that the best part for Nirvaan is not any particular cracker but the time spent doing activities with family and friends. A shop-bought cracker may be over in a second, but this one gives children the chance to build, play and repeat the experience. Making sustainability a part of the celebration The popsicle-stick crackers are just one part of the family's efforts to make Diwali more mindful. Swati has also switched to battery-operated diyas, which give the home a festive glow without the worry of open flames around two toddlers. For rangoli, she opts for organic colours, keeping in mind that the boys often end up touching and playing with them. The family also makes its own paper lanterns, garlands and bandanwars instead of buying plastic decorations. For Swati, these activities offer children a chance to participate in the preparations rather than simply watch the adults do everything. From battery-operated diyas to organic rangoli colours, the family has found simple ways to make its festive celebrations more mindful. When it comes to explaining why the family chooses alternatives to noisy crackers , she keeps the conversation age-appropriate. "At their age you can't explain AQI or pollution. I tell them smoke hurts our eyes, and the doggies get scared of loud bangs. That's enough for them to understand," she says. She is also careful not to make the children feel that celebrating sustainably means missing out. They still enjoy a few traditional crackers with their parents, while the homemade ones add another layer of fun. A little change can make Diwali more meaningful Swati's idea has also caught the attention of other parents. Several families who saw her homemade crackers have tried making them with their own children. She believes such small changes can influence how children understand celebrations and their relationship with the environment. "Kids learn from what we do, not from what we tell them," she says. When children make something themselves and enjoy it just as much, they begin to understand that having fun does not have to come at the cost of the air, animals or anyone's health. For Swati, the idea is to show her children that celebrating Diwali can be just as joyful with a few thoughtful changes and activities made together at home. Her advice to parents looking to make their festivities more sustainable is simple: start small. "You don't have to stop crackers completely. Keep a few, skip the excess, and add one thing you make with your kids. Once they've made something with their own hands, they won't miss the rest," she says. And perhaps that is what makes this family's Diwali special. Between colourful sticks, handmade decorations and little bursts of laughter, the boys are discovering that some of the best festive memories are not bought from a shop. They are made together at home. All images courtesy of Swati Jain

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Vietnamese Farmers Built a Rice Straw Circular Economy that Pays Reading Time: 3 minutes A rice straw circular economy in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta turns leftover stalks into mushrooms and compost. Rice straw circular economy models give Vietnamese farmers a reason to stop burning their fields. At New Green Farm Cooperative in the Mekong Delta, leftover stalks now feed mushroom beds and compost piles. As a result, member farmers have cut their use of chemical nitrogen fertilizer by 40%. The cooperative works with about 100 farming households across 148 hectares. In its operating area, straw burning has dropped by 90-95%. Farmers are earning more while their fields send up far less smoke. Burning has long been the default after harvest. It clears fields quickly and costs nothing up front. It also fills the air with smoke and dust and releases planet-warming gases. A circular economy offers another path. It keeps materials in use, so one process’s waste becomes the next one’s raw material. In a rice straw circular economy, the stalks become food, fertilizer, and income. New Green Farm put this idea to work in 2023, starting with seven core members. Director Dong Van Canh partnered with the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) through the RiceEco project. The Mekong-Republic of Korea Cooperation Fund pays for RiceEco, which supports Vietnam’s One Million Hectares program for low-emission rice. After harvest, a local machinery company bales the straw with mechanized equipment. The cooperative grows mushrooms on about 9,000 bales a year, or roughly 25 a day. Straw also goes into compost, which returns nutrients to the rice fields. That compost explains the drop in chemical fertilizer. Using less fertilizer saves farmers USD 57 to 65 per hectare each season. Selling their straw adds another USD 13 to 15 per hectare per crop. For the cooperative, each mushroom bale earns about 38 US cents in profit, or roughly USD 3,400 a year. Compost adds about USD 2,700 a year, or USD 38 per ton for 72 tons. Canh says the model gives farmers more than one way to earn. Rice still brings in about 60% of the cooperative’s income, while mushrooms add about 30%. Compost, vegetables, and other products make up the rest. In a rice straw circular economy, farmers grow more than rice and cultivate new income sources. Rice provides about 60% of the cooperative’s earnings, while mushrooms contribute another 30%, with compost, vegetables, and other products filling out the rest. Photo by Petr Ganaj on Pexels. That income mix has helped the business grow. Operating space has expanded from 2,500 to about 11,000 square meters, roughly two American football fields. Products now reach buyers in Ho Chi Minh City and on Phu Quoc Island. Canh’s role has changed over time. He moved from field labor to organizing production, managing staff, and finding buyers. His wife runs the cooperative’s onion and chili pepper plots. Other cooperatives in the delta are seeing similar results. In Can Tho, the Tien Thuan Agricultural and Service Cooperative received straw balers and composting machines in June 2024. By September 2025, it was producing 12 to 15 tons of organic fertilizer a month. Circular methods there add USD 50 to 70 of value per hectare. Burning straw or selling it loose adds only about USD 25. The cooperative’s mushroom houses produce up to 1,050 kilograms every six weeks. Farmers there report that field crabs and earthworms have returned, both signs of healthier soil. The work has also created new jobs, especially for women. Machines now handle much of the heavy labor of clearing fields. An estimated 30 to 40% of nearby farmers have adopted similar methods. That uptake matters, because a rice straw circular economy depends on many farms supplying straw. The approach also works outside the delta. In northern Ninh Binh Province, the Nam Cuong cooperative composts rice straw with cow manure for its potatoes. A mechanized turner has cut composting time from 90 days to 45. Potato fields that received this compost yielded 19 to 28 tons per hectare. Plots without it needed 20% more potassium and nitrogen fertilizer. The cooperative now supplies organic produce to meal programs at 20 local schools. Growth has exposed some weak points. New Green Farm faces cash-flow gaps between harvests and limited capital to expand. Storage space also runs short during peak seasons. Affordable loans and better baling equipment would help close those gaps. The cooperative plans larger warehouses for straw collection. Project partners also aim to bring the model to other cooperatives. RiceEco has already brought the rice straw circular economy to 5,084 farmers and other stakeholders. It supports four pilot businesses in Vietnam and Cambodia. Its work also informed Vietnam’s 2023 national guideline on sustainable rice straw management. For generations, people saw straw as something to get rid of. Cooperatives like New Green Farm have turned it into mushrooms, compost, and steady income. The rice straw circular economy shows that the answer to field burning can also be a business plan. The post How Vietnamese Farmers Built a Rice Straw Circular Economy that Pays appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News From Climate Disasters to Resilient Cities: Connecting Technology, Nature, and Communities Reading Time: 3 minutes From Texas floods to Himalayan glacier collapse, cities built for a climate that no longer exists are discovering that real resilience means connecting technology, nature, and people, not just adding more sensors. Before dawn on July 4, 2025, the Guadalupe River at Kerrville rose from about 3 feet to 30 feet in just 45 minutes, turning part of the Texas Hill Country into a disaster zone. In August 2026, a glacier collapse near the Nepal-Tibet border triggered catastrophic flooding that damaged settlements, roads and hydropower infrastructure. Toronto and Southern Ontario have faced their own warning signs. In July 2024, intense rainfall flooded highways and subway stations, while a major power outage affected nearly 300,000 customers. Canada’s 2026 wildfire season has also forced evacuations. These events are geographically different, but they expose a common vulnerability: many cities were built for a climate that no longer exists. Infrastructure designed around historical weather conditions is increasingly being tested by more intense rainfall, extreme heat, wildfires and other climate hazards. We are also pushing against planetary limits. The pressure is broader than climate change alone. The 2025 Planetary Health Check found that seven of the nine planetary boundaries have been crossed, including climate change, freshwater change, biosphere integrity, and ocean acidification. These pressures interact. Damage to ecosystems can weaken carbon sinks, while climate change can disrupt freshwater cycles. In 2026, the United Nations University warned of “global water bankruptcy,” describing water systems so depleted or degraded that they may no longer easily return to historical conditions. For cities, these pressures quickly become infrastructure challenges. Extreme rainfall overwhelms stormwater systems. Heat stresses buildings, electricity grids and public health. Drought and groundwater depletion threaten water security. This is why mitigation and adaptation cannot be treated as separate agendas. Mitigation reduces the emissions driving future warming. Adaptation reduces impacts that are already occurring or can no longer be fully avoided. Yet adaptation has a major financing problem. UNEP estimates that developing countries will need about US$310 billion to US$365 billion annually by 2035, while international public adaptation finance flows were only US$26 billion in 2023. Adaptation needs are now roughly 12 to 14 times current flows. Resilience plans cannot remain on paper when cities need drainage, cooling, early-warning and water systems now. What does a climate-resilient city actually look like? Smart buildings can reduce energy demand through efficient design, sensors and automated controls while improving thermal comfort and indoor air quality. At the neighbourhood scale, renewables, storage, microgrids and electric mobility can reduce emissions while strengthening resilience. Internet of Things, or IoT, technologies can monitor rainfall, drainage, temperature and infrastructure performance. But a community is not “smart” simply because it has more sensors. Some of the most powerful solutions work with natural systems. Low-impact development and sustainable stormwater management use rain gardens, bioswales, permeable pavements, green roofs, infiltration areas, and rainwater harvesting to retain, absorb, filter, or reuse rainfall close to where it falls. Blue-green infrastructure extends this through wetlands, urban forests, ponds, and waterways. The principle is simple: instead of designing cities only to move water away as quickly as possible, we can design them to absorb, store, filter, and reuse it. Blue-green infrastructure shifts urban water management from moving rainfall away as fast as possible to absorbing, storing, filtering, and reusing it through rain gardens, bioswales, wetlands, green roofs, and urban forests built into the city fabric. Photo by Shox Art on Pexels. Bangladesh offers a powerful community-level example. In salinity-affected coastal areas, women trained as “Pani Apas,” or water sisters, help households use and maintain rainwater-harvesting systems. The model does more than provide water tanks. It connects climate adaptation with safer water, women’s livelihoods, skills and community ownership. UNDP reports that related coastal initiatives provide year-round safe drinking water to nearly 140,000 people in parts of Khulna and Satkhira. Costa Rica offers a different lesson from Latin America. Since 2015, nearly all of its electricity has come from renewable sources, with hydropower supplying around 70%, alongside wind and geothermal power. Yet prolonged dry periods increasingly challenge hydropower production. Costa Rica therefore illustrates why mitigation and adaptation must advance together. A clean electricity system still needs diversified renewables, resilient grids and water-aware planning. The five Ps of sustainable development, People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, and Partnership, provide a useful way to judge these solutions. People ask who is protected. Planet asks whether emissions, water, and ecosystems are considered together. Prosperity asks whether investment creates livelihoods and resilient infrastructure. Peace brings in fairness, trust and accountable institutions. Partnership recognizes that governments, communities, engineers, businesses and civil society organizations must work together. The major gap today is often not the absence of solutions. It is our failure to connect them, finance them adequately, implement them equitably and maintain them over time. Sensors can warn us that water is rising. Blue-green infrastructure can help absorb it. Rainwater harvesting can turn rainfall into a resource. Clean electricity can reduce emissions. But people still need the knowledge, resources and authority to operate these systems and shape the decisions behind them. A truly smart and resilient city is not the one with the most connected devices. It is the one that connects technology, nature, infrastructure and people well enough to reduce risk before disaster occurs, protect the most vulnerable and recover more equitably when disruption cannot be avoided. The post From Climate Disasters to Resilient Cities: Connecting Technology, Nature, and Communities appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Karl Bushby left Chile on foot in 1998 at age 29, with golden hair and two iron rules: no machines to carry him forward, and no coming home — not for illness, not for grief, not for anything. Twenty-eight years, 75 million steps, one polar bear encounter, 31 days swimming the Caspian Sea, and a jail cell in Panama later, he walked up to his mother's house in Hull, England, pushing the same cart he'd had for a quarter century. The cheers fell quiet at the doorstep. What lingers most isn't the staggering mileage but the strange disorientation of arrival — he found himself looking the wrong way crossing the road in his own country, a foreigner in his birthplace. "I'm home, but it's not the home that I'm used to now for so long," he said. "I almost feel guilt." Nearly half his life spent walking the earth had multiplied his sense of belonging until home meant something far larger and more complicated than a red-brick terrace in northern England. His parting thought wasn't about endurance or willpower — it was a quiet insistence that the world is full of people who have drastically underestimated themselves, and that the first step is simply imagining otherwise.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Upcycling Food Industry Byproducts into Ingredients People Want to Eat Reading Time: 3 minutes Upcycling food industry byproducts turns factory leftovers into tasty, useful ingredients. Dutch company Greencovery shows how this can work for food makers. Upcycling food industry byproducts means turning leftover material from food factories into new ingredients. Food makers often call these leftovers side streams. Many side streams end up discarded or sold as animal feed. Greencovery , a company based in Wageningen in the Netherlands, wants to change that. It says its patented technology recovers valuable ingredients from side streams. The goal is to create new revenue for manufacturers and a lighter footprint on the planet. The scale of food waste is large. The UN Environment Programme reported that the world wasted 1.05 billion metric tons of food in 2022. That equals about 19% of the food available to consumers. Those figures cover homes, restaurants, and stores, not factory leftovers. Still, they show why finding new uses for food matters. Food loss and waste also affect the climate. The same report links it to 8% to 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions. That is almost five times the emissions from the aviation sector. A side stream is the material left after a factory makes its main product. That material often still holds useful compounds. Greencovery focuses on pulling those compounds out and returning them to the food supply. Animal feed is a common destination for these leftovers. Greencovery describes it as a lower-value outcome than human food. Its team sees upcycling food industry byproducts as a way to move more material toward food ingredients. The company uses what it calls mild separation technology. Separation means pulling the useful parts out of a mixture. Mild means gentle conditions, and the company says the method uses less energy and water than other separation techniques. Why does that matter? The company says the ingredients it extracts carry a low carbon footprint. A carbon footprint measures the greenhouse gases released to make a product. The recovered ingredients bring three listed strengths: high functionality, great taste, and microbial stability. Functionality means an ingredient performs well in recipes. Microbial stability means it resists spoilage by microbes and holds up in storage. Upcycling food industry byproducts turns okara, the often-overlooked soy pulp left after soy milk or tofu production, into Okara Pro and Okara Tex, two neutral-tasting, nutritious ingredients suited to bakery goods, savory dishes, and plant-based meat. Photo by Polina Tankilevitch on Pexels. Greencovery does not stop at the lab. It guides partners through three checkpoints for upcycling food industry byproducts. Each one answers a question. Does it work? Does the market want it? Is it commercially viable? The first checkpoint is a proof of concept, which tests whether the idea works technically. The team also runs early product trials to see if a side stream can become a functional ingredient. Next comes a proof of market, which checks whether buyers want the product. The team tests taste, function, and nutrition. It also brings potential buyers into the conversation early. The final step is a proof of business. It covers pricing, costs, profit margins, and supply chains. Greencovery also co-invests with partners and helps set up production in a suitable location. The team blends technology experts, food application specialists, and business experts. Together, they test both the science and the numbers. Two real products show upcycling food industry byproducts at work. The company has made a high-fiber satay sauce and a Parmigiano Reggiano mayonnaise. Both reflect its aim of using ingredients that might otherwise be discarded. The Dutch Prime Minister met the team and experienced both products firsthand. The meeting took place during the Netherlands’ food waste awareness week. Foodvalley NL, a group that promotes innovation and sustainability in food, invited Greencovery to the event. The talks focused on cutting food waste and finding better uses for ingredients. Greencovery also thanked the Upcycling Community for its support. Greencovery says it works to speed up the path from idea to market. Faster launches help companies see returns sooner. Manufacturers curious about their own side streams can start small. Greencovery offers a free 30-minute consultation call. These claims come from Greencovery itself, so readers should treat them as company-reported. Food makers considering upcycling their food byproducts should run their own trials and check local food safety rules before launching a product. Shoppers can play a part too. Choosing upcycled foods signals demand, which encourages more companies to try. Shoppers interested in upcycling food industry byproducts should read labels closely. A product can earn the upcycled label with only 10% upcycled ingredients by weight, so it helps to learn what the upcycled label actually requires. Organic foods, by comparison, must contain at least 95% certified organic ingredients. Food waste remains a large problem, but practical tools to shrink it are taking shape. Upcycling food industry byproducts gives manufacturers a clear path from leftover to ingredient. With testing, market checks, and careful planning, a side stream can become a product people choose to buy. The post Upcycling Food Industry Byproducts into Ingredients People Want to Eat appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.titleOriginal: AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage
items.description: Οι ερευνητές του Stanford ανακάλυψαν ένα φυσικό μόριο που προσδιορίζεται από την τεχνητή νοημοσύνη που καταστέλλει δραματικά την όρεξη και προάγει την απώλεια λίπους στα ζώα, προσφέροντας πιθανώς μια θεραπεία απώλειας βάρους παρόμοια με το Ozempic χωρίς κοινές πεπτικές παρενέργειες ή σημαντική απώλεια μυών. Ονομάζεται BRP, το μόριο μείωσε την πρόσληψη τροφής έως και 50% και στοχεύει διαφορετικά…
items.descriptionOriginal: Stanford researchers have discovered an AI-identified natural molecule that dramatically suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, potentially offering an Ozempic-like weight-loss treatment without common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss. Called BRP, the molecule reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful.
