items.descriptionOriginal: A few tulsi leaves in a cup of hot water, a handful in homemade kadha , or a plant growing in a sunny balcony corner. In many Indian households, tulsi is familiar in all these forms . Its fragrant leaves have been used in traditional home remedies, herbal drinks, and everyday household practices, making it one of the most recognisable herbs grown at home. November is a good time to turn our attention to this plant. As the monsoon recedes and cooler weather sets in across much of India, families reach for warm herbal drinks and traditional preparations. Tulsi can be grown in pots or garden beds, making fresh leaves easily accessible for everyday use. It needs some protection from cold weather in frost-prone areas, but generally grows well with adequate sunlight and well-drained soil. Known by its botanical name, Ocimum tenuiflorum, it is also called holy basil. It has a long history in Ayurveda and contains aromatic compounds that have attracted scientific interest. From the kitchen to traditional household practices, here are some of the many ways this familiar plant is used. 1. A common ingredient in home remedies When someone develops a cough or complains of a sore throat, tulsi leaves may be among the first ingredients taken out of the garden. They are mostly used in homemade kadha , often alongside ginger, black pepper, and other kitchen ingredients. Tulsi can be grown in pots or garden beds, making fresh leaves easily accessible for everyday use. Photograph: (Image generated by AI) A systematic review published in 2017 in Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine examined human studies on tulsi and reported promising findings in areas including stress and metabolic health. The researchers also highlighted the need for more rigorous studies. Traditional use does not establish that tulsi can cure infections or replace medical treatment. 2. Adding flavour to tea and herbal drinks A few fresh tulsi leaves can lend a distinctive aroma to a cup of tea. Some households add them to regular chai with ginger, while others steep the leaves in hot water to prepare a simple herbal infusion. These drinks are particularly appealing on chilly November mornings and evenings. Having this plant at home means fresh leaves are within easy reach whenever someone wants to make a cup. The leaves have a strong flavour, so a small quantity is usually enough. Ginger, lemon, and other ingredients can be added according to personal preference. 3. A source of aromatic essential oil Crush a tulsi leaf gently between your fingers , and its fragrance becomes immediately noticeable. The scent comes from volatile compounds present in the plant, including eugenol. Its aromatic properties have attracted interest beyond traditional household use. Its essential oil and constituent compounds have been studied for potential applications in medicinal products, flavours, and fragrances. A 2015 release from the Government of India's Press Information Bureau , discussing research into the tulsi genome by CSIR scientists, highlighted the plant's potential for further scientific and commercial applications. 4. Studied for its insect-repellent properties The plant has long been associated with keeping insects away in traditional household practices. Researchers have investigated the insect-repellent properties of its essential oil and certain compounds found in the plant. Known by its botanical name, Ocimum tenuiflorum, it is also called holy basil. Photograph: (Organicbazar) However, there is a difference between testing concentrated oils under controlled conditions and growing this plant in a pot. The presence of the plant alone cannot be relied upon to protect a home from mosquitoes. Bed nets, window screens, and proven repellents remain more dependable ways to prevent bites. 5. A traditional addition to grain storage Before modern storage products became widely available, households relied on different plant materials in their efforts to protect stored food. Tulsi leaves have been mentioned in traditional practices involving stored grains, where their aroma was believed to discourage insects. Such practices reflect how families used plants available around them to address everyday needs. However, its leaves should not replace proper grain drying, airtight containers, or established methods of preventing pest infestations. 6. A plant that can be grown in small spaces The plant does not require a large garden. A pot placed in a sunny spot can be enough to grow the plant, provided it has well-draining soil and receives suitable care. November can be a comfortable time for gardening in many parts of India after the rains have ended. It generally benefits from sunlight and moderate watering, but it needs protection from frost and harsh cold in colder regions. Waterlogged soil should be avoided, as it can damage the roots. Regularly checking the leaves for pests and removing damaged growth can help keep the plant healthy. Once established, it can provide fresh leaves for household use without taking up much space. 7. Used in traditional wellness practices Tulsi has also received attention for its possible role in supporting general wellbeing. A systematic review published in 2017 examined studies involving human participants and found preliminary evidence of benefits relating to stress, mood, and certain metabolic measures. Tulsi leaves have been mentioned in traditional practices involving stored grains, where their aroma was believed to discourage insects. Photograph: (MagicBricks) The findings are interesting, but they do not mean that drinking tulsi tea or eating its leaves will necessarily produce these effects. The studies varied in their methods and preparations, and more research is needed to establish appropriate doses, long-term safety, and effectiveness. For households that already grow this plant, its place in traditional wellness practices is another reason the plant has remained popular. It is important, however, to distinguish between customary use and benefits established through clinical research. As November brings cooler mornings to many parts of the country, the humble plant offers a timely reminder of how much can come from a single pot in the garden .

items.title: «Θέλω να σπουδάσω, όχι να παντρευτώ»: Πώς μια 19χρονη και άλλες γυναίκες αντιστάθηκαν στο έθιμο του Rajasthan Bride-Exchange
items.titleOriginal: ‘I Want To Study, Not Marry’: How a 19-YO & Other Women Stood up to Rajasthan’s Bride-Exchange Custom
items.description: Στα 14 της, η Monica Jod είχε ήδη αρχίσει να καταλαβαίνει ότι η ζωή που της σχεδίαζαν δεν ήταν εντελώς δική της. Είχε έρθει στο Sambhali Trust αφού της αρνήθηκαν την ευκαιρία να σπουδάσει. Στο σπίτι, μεγάλωσε ακούγοντας ότι ένα αγόρι ήταν το φως της οικογένειας: "Ladka Ghar ka chirag" . Ούτε οι γυναίκες γύρω της υποστήριξαν την επιθυμία της για εκπαίδευση. Γάμος…
items.descriptionOriginal: At 14, Monica Jod had already begun to understand that the life being planned for her was not entirely hers. She had come to Sambhali Trust after being denied the chance to study. At home, she grew up hearing that a boy was the light of the family: "Ladka Ghar ka chirag" . The women around her did not support her wish for education either. Marriage, like so many other decisions affecting girls, seemed to belong to the family. But Monica did not accept that this was where her choices ended. She left home four times over the course of her life. Each time, she was trying to move further away from the idea that a woman's place was fixed by marriage, family expectations and domestic responsibilities. Years later, at 35, Monica works with women who are trying to make the same journey. Some arrive at Sambhali Trust after being caught in a marriage arrangement where leaving one household can have consequences for another woman. "Their marriages are not treated as separate relationships. They are tied together by a custom known as atta-satta," says Govind Singh Rathore, founder of Jodhpur-based Sambhali Trust. In parts of Rajasthan, a woman's marriage is a family bargain. The practice came under legal scrutiny in Rajasthan this year when the Rajasthan High Court, while hearing a matrimonial dispute, criticised atta-satta and described the arrangement as a form of "mutual hostage-taking" between families. Photograph: (Sambhali Trust) "A daughter is married into one household while a daughter from that household is married to her brother, or another male member of her family. The two marriages are negotiated together. What happens in one can affect the other," Rathore explains. And that is where the arrangement can become a trap. Your marriage does not belong only to you This is the part of atta-satta that is often missed when the custom is described simply as an exchange of marriage relationships . Its most consequential feature is not only that two marriages are arranged together, but that one woman's choices can be used as leverage against another. Rathore has spent years working with women caught in such situations. He says the practice remains particularly prevalent in parts of western Rajasthan even today, including the desert districts of Barmer, Bikaner and Jodhpur. The consequences, he says, can be devastating. "Women as young as 19 are married to men in their 50s or 60s, and their lives often spiral into cycles of abuse, violence and neglect," he says. His own family members have been impacted by it. But nearly 19 years since Sambhali Trust began working with women and girls in Rajasthan in 2007, the need for its intervention remains evident in the cases it continues to handle.Photograph: (Sambhali Trust) "I was married at 15, when my wife was just 14. We later had a social marriage when I was 19 and she was 18," Rathore recalls. His own experience, he says, is part of a larger reality. He remembers a German visitor observing, "There are no adolescent girls in Rajasthan!" It showed how many girls are pushed into adulthood before their time, burdened with responsibilities and denied the freedom to experience adolescence. When marriages become linked Families may believe that exchanging daughters reduces the financial burden associated with marriage, including dowry or dahej . But reciprocity has another side. Imagine a woman leaving her husband. Under an ordinary marriage, the dispute would concern her, her husband and their respective families. In an atta-satta arrangement, her decision can be presented as a breach of an agreement between households. Her family may be told that if she does not return, the other family will send their daughter back. "If one woman faces violence, another woman can automatically become vulnerable to violence too," Rathore says. The cost of saying no The custom continues not because every family necessarily sees women as commodities , Rathore says, but because the arrangement is woven into economic and social structures that can be difficult for families to challenge. "People are looking at everything materially," Rathore says. "But a girl is not a material object." For families with limited resources, the promise of reducing marriage expenses can make atta-satta appear rational. But what begins as an economic arrangement can create a form of social indebtedness in which women are expected to honour an agreement they never made themselves. "Women are naturally looking for some kind of respite, some way out of difficult circumstances. But the same system can turn against them," he says. Rathore recalls a case that came to Sambhali Trust involving a young woman whose family had entered into an atta-satta arrangement. Certain conditions had been attached to her brother's marriage, and she had agreed to the arrangement. But soon after her brother got married, she left home with the man she wanted to be with. Her decision did not end the matter. According to Rathore, members of her community hunted her down, while her parents came under pressure to settle the dispute through the local panchayat. The family was expected to pay a substantial amount as part of the settlement. Rathore also says local intermediaries or agents involved in facilitating such arrangements can demand amounts running into Rs 10–15 lakh, after which a woman may still be forced back into a marriage she does not want. A custom under scrutiny The practice came under legal scrutiny in Rajasthan this year when the Rajasthan High Court, while hearing a matrimonial dispute, criticised atta-satta and described the arrangement as a form of "mutual hostage-taking" between families. The observation put into words the problem faced by women working with such cases. The Better India reached out to Kumkum Thanvi, a counselling psychologist and psycho-oncologist working with Sambhali Trust's Nirbhaya Initiative. Launched in 2014, the initiative is an emergency assistance system that connects survivors with in-house psychologists, medical teams and legal advisers to guide them through rights education and court processes. Thanvi says, "It usually takes three to four sessions to help families understand that if one marriage is facing difficulties due to incompatibility, conflict or violence, it does not mean that the other marriage should also be ended. This is one of the major challenges associated with the atta-satta marriage practice. Legally, we follow the same legal procedures and provide the same legal guidance as we would in any other marriage-related case." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sambhali Trust (@sambhalitrust) But what happens when a woman approaches the Trust seeking to leave an abusive marriage? "First, I try to understand the woman's situation, explain her rights, assess her immediate safety needs and help her explore the options available to her, without pressuring her into any particular decision. This could include approaching the police if she faces threats, physical violence, harassment, confinement or coercion; seeking protection under the Domestic Violence Act, 2005, in cases of domestic abuse; or approaching the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) for free legal assistance, including guidance on separation or divorce." But knowing one's rights does not automatically make leaving possible. Thanvi identifies financial dependence, concerns about children's custody and education, family pressure and the prospect of lengthy legal proceedings as some of the biggest barriers women encounter. "Simply telling a woman to leave her marriage is not enough," she says. "She also needs to know where she will go, how she will support herself and her children, and who will stand by her afterwards." That is the point at which custom collides with individual freedom. Rathore, too, believes this is why the issue cannot be addressed only through individual interventions. "That is why there is no point blaming the police or the families entirely," he says. "The real solution has to begin with changing the mindset." 'You cannot give away girls in the name of tradition' Rathore sees education and economic independence as central to that change. One argument used to justify atta-satta is that exchanging daughters can ease the financial burden of marriage and dowry. But Rathore says that reasoning obscures what is being exchanged. A woman is not an economic counterweight to another marriage. The situation becomes more serious when children are brought into such arrangements. "Girls as young as nine or 10 are being bound into atta-satta arrangements," he says. Rathore also points to Rajasthan's skewed sex ratio as one of the factors contributing to the continuation of reciprocal marriages. With fewer girls available within communities, families can increasingly turn to arrangements such as atta-satta to secure marriages for their sons. But stopping the practice requires more than telling families not to exchange daughters. It requires giving girls and women alternatives. "People need to understand that a daughter is not something that can be exchanged," he says. The way out begins before the crisis This is where Sambhali Trust's work moves beyond rescuing women from individual marriages. The organisation's name, Sambhali, refers to the "rising of deprived women". Its approach centres on helping women and girls become independent enough that they no longer need the organisation to survive. Education is one part of that work. Vocational training is another. For women facing domestic violence, the organisation runs a shelter home service where they can find a safe place to stay while receiving counselling, support and advice. It also assists women who want to pursue justice through the courts. View this post on Instagram A post shared by 𝘼𝙫𝙣𝙚𝙚𝙩 (@avneetsun) A woman who has access to these things has more choices. "The ultimate aim should be to make women independent," Rathore says. "They should reach a point where they don't need Sambhali anymore." But nearly 19 years since Sambhali Trust began working with women and girls in Rajasthan in 2007, the need for its intervention remains evident in the cases it continues to handle. Between April 2025 and March 2026, the Trust received 956 helpline calls, handled 188 cases through psychological counselling and legal guidance, and provided temporary shelter to 14 high-risk survivors. Among them was 19-year-old Nisha (name changed), whose brothers attempted to force her into an atta-satta marriage in April 2025 to secure a bride for themselves in return. When Nisha resisted, she faced severe physical and emotional abuse, leaving both her and her mother without support. She eventually approached the National Commission for Women, which helped secure her rescue and placement with Sambhali Trust. Under the care of project psychologist Dr Deepti, she found a safe space to recover and speak about the future she wanted. "I want to study, not marry," she said. During an intensive family mediation session, Nisha faced further pressure from relatives to return home. But she stood her ground and chose independence. Today, she remains under the Trust's protection and is pursuing the education she was nearly forced to give up. Monica chose differently Monica knows what that independence can mean because she had to build it herself. At 14, she came to Sambhali Trust after being denied the opportunity to study. The women in her own family did not support her either. But her father, along with Sambhali Trust founder Govind Singh Rathore, encouraged her to pursue education and build a life of her own. Monica left home four times over the course of her life. "I was trying to escape the idea that her future had already been decided," Monica tells The Better India . "I wanted to come out of the thinking that women are nothing." Years later, her efforts earned her the Gargi Puraskar, a recognition for girls who perform exceptionally in education. The Gargi Puraskar (Gargi Award) is a Rajasthan State Government incentive scheme that rewards meritorious female students who secure exceptional scores in their Class 10 and 12 board examinations. When she told Rathore about the award, he encouraged her to attend the ceremony. Monica was hesitant. Monica had come to Sambhali Trust after being denied the chance to study. At home, she grew up hearing that a boy was the light of the family: "Ladka Ghar ka chirag". Photograph: (Sambhali Trust) Rathore told her, "Go, and take your mother with you." Her mother went. For Monica, the moment marked a change in their relationship. Years of conditioning began to loosen, and her mother finally told her: "You do what you want. I will not force you into marriage. Live your life." That sentence had been missing from Monica's childhood: permission to decide for herself. Today, at 35, she works with women who arrive at Sambhali facing restrictions she once experienced. Some are victims of atta-satta. Monica helps them navigate the process when they need to file complaints or follow up on cases. She tells them to build the ability to choose. "If education stops, learn vocational skills. Learn anything you can," she says. "Even if you earn Rs 2,000 or Rs 3,000, earn something. And keep some of that money for yourself. Save at least Rs 200." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kathy Gerber (@kathygerberphoto) A little savings can mean the ability to make a phone call, travel somewhere, seek help or make a decision without asking someone else for money. "Education and money can only help us," she says. Monica also understands why many women do not immediately recognise that they have a choice. "Women don't have exposure, so they don't realise the worth of freedom," she says. That is perhaps the deeper challenge facing atta-satta. The custom does not survive only through the moment a marriage is arranged. It survives through the expectations surrounding that marriage: the belief that a daughter must protect the family's agreement, that a sister must bear the consequences of her brother's marriage, and that another woman's future can be used to keep her from leaving. Breaking that chain therefore requires changing what women believe they are allowed to ask for. For Monica, the answer began with a classroom she had once been told she could not enter.

items.descriptionOriginal: Recommendations are independently selected by our team but may result in a commission to Nice News which helps keep our content free. Nice News readers know there’s no shortage of nice things in the world, and that includes products that make our lives a little better and brighter. In that spirit, we’re excited to share this roundup of our team’s favorite items from the past year — things we actually purchased (or received as gifts) and have loved using. For 2026, we’ve got an unbeatable hair brush, a cordless vacuum, scented bookmarks, and more. Combined, these 20 products comprise a pretty great holiday shopping guide, if we do say so ourselves. Scroll down for stocking stuffer ideas, big-ticket splurges, and practical presents that can be found in our team’s kitchens, closets, and makeup drawers. Ally, Staff Editor: Lykke Copper Interchangeable Knitting Needles Courtesy of Revolution Fibers Shop revolution fibers Shop Amazon This was my first “big” purchase after learning how to knit and getting a few projects under my belt. So far it’s been completely worth it — beyond looking beautiful, the copper needles offer the smoothness of stainless steel while conducting heat better, which I’ve read may make them easier on your joints (though there isn’t solid science to back that up). The set comes with every needle size a beginner could need, plus some interchangeable cords and a vegan suede case. Le Creuset Heritage Butter Dish Courtesy of Le Creuset Shop LE CREUSET Shop Amazon I received this adorable butter dish as a gift, and highly recommend giving it as one. It’s a relatively inexpensive way into the wide, wonderful world of Le Creuset ceramics and looks good in any kitchen. I have it in the deep yellow Nectar hue, but there are several other colors to choose from. Dyson Paddle Hairbrush Courtesy of Dyson Shop DYSON SHOP WALMART Dyson gets a lot of hype for its powerful blow dryers, but I’m here to sing the praises of the company’s humble hairbrush. Sure, it’s more expensive than the ones you can grab at a drugstore, but for something I use every day, it’s a major upgrade. My hair feels silky smooth, the bristles navigate knots with ease, and it has that signature sleek Dyson design. Brett, Senior Account Manager: Levoit Cordless Vacuum Cleaner Courtesy of Levoit Shop LEVOIT SHOP AMAZON My cordless vacuum is easily one of my favorite purchases this year. I love how convenient and lightweight it is, making it extremely easy to quickly clean up my everyday messes without having to drag out a bulky vacuum or worry about cords. Turtlebox Original (Gen 3) Speaker Courtesy of Turtlebox Shop TURTLEBOX SHOP AMAZON This Bluetooth speaker has been perfect for everything from backyard parties to beach days, with impressive sound quality and durability that’s truly second to none. The best part is knowing I can bring it anywhere without having to worry about it getting knocked around or damaged. Josh, Content Strategist: Apple Airpods 4 Courtesy of Apple Shop AMAZON The AirPods 4 with active noise cancellation have become my preferred choice for work. Their noise cancellation performs noticeably better than other earbuds I own. I use them to block out background sounds without playing any music, and they’ve significantly boosted my focus and productivity. UGREEN Wireless Mouse 2.4G Courtesy of UGREEN Shop Amazon As someone who dislikes touchpads, this mouse has been a lifesaver. Setup was effortless, it’s super responsive, comfortable, and ergonomic, and the battery life is amazing — I’ve only needed to charge it a few times since March! Marika, Contributing Writer: Solar Rainbow Maker Window Charm Courtesy of Uncommon Goods Shop UNCOMMON GOODS Shop AMAZON ​I’m amazed by this rainbow maker! It hangs on a window in the sunniest nook of our home and scatters rainbows across the kitchen. It’s so magical that even my dog seems to get a kick out of looking at the colors (or maybe watching me get a kick out of them ). Highly recommend scrolling through the customer reviews to see examples of it in action. Violette_FR Bisou Balm Lipstick Courtesy of Violette_FR shop violette_fr SHOP SEPHORA Bisou Balm made me a lipstick person. I love the matte “blush for the lips” look and it smells like a waffle. I have it in Rose Latte and I’m tempted to try the bestseller Bêtise, but I don’t want to mess with a good thing! Thule Sapling Baby Backpack Courtesy of Thule Shop THULE This backpack baby carrier is my favorite thing from my baby registry. It feels so secure and gives me peace of mind knowing my daughter is tucked in and protected from the sun while we hike uphill, downhill, wherever. And she seems to love the view! The bottom compartment is also surprisingly roomy and fits everything we need when we leave the house, which is a lot. Mike, SVP, Editorial Strategy Aftelier Perfumes Biblioscents Scented Bookmarks Courtesy of Aftelier Perfumes Shop AMAZON Shop Aftelier PErfumes If you love to read and were mildly obsessed with scratch-and-sniff stickers as a kid, consider ditching the dog-ears for a four-pack of Biblioscents. Scratching the botanical illustration on each bookmark releases a grown-up scent — ginger root, frankincense, vetiver, geranium — for an adult version of an old habit. Natalie, Senior Managing Editor YQh Retractable Sink Storage Rack Courtesy of YQh Shop AMAZON You know those products you didn’t realize you needed until you discovered they existed? This retractable sink rack is on that list. After having purchased multiple sink caddies that left water pooling by the kitchen faucet, I wanted an organizer that freed up space and didn’t require me to wipe down the countertop every time I washed a dish. This rack is exactly what I was (unknowingly) looking for: It expands over the sink, allowing water from the soap dispenser and sponge to drip directly down the drain. It’s also stainless steel and has a slim design with anti-slip rubber sleeves that help keep it in place. Plank+Beam Contour Console Table Courtesy of Plank + Beam Shop plank + Beam Shop Amazon I’d been on the hunt for a console table for months and fell in love with this one from Plank+Beam as soon as I saw it. It’s constructed of solid pine wood, easy to assemble, and the perfect height and length for my narrow entryway (I got the 56-inch length, but it’s also available in 46 inches). It comes in three wood finishes and looks extremely high-end but sells at a much lower price point than comparable options from well-known furniture stores. Tovolo Mini Ice Squeeze-and-Release Cylinders Courtesy of Tovolo Shop AMAZON If you’re a fan of nugget ice but aren’t ready to splurge on a sleek countertop maker , these squeeze-and-release ice cylinders are a great alternative. They come in a set of two and each makes 200 mini ice cubes — ideal for one to two drinks at a time, depending on how cold you prefer your beverage. I like that they’re compact, BPA-free and dishwasher-safe, and that I can enjoy mini ice nuggets more regularly without a machine. Rebekah, Staff Editor: Levi’s Men’s Chino Tech Pants Courtesy of Levi’s Shop AMAZON My husband wanted some casual but elevated pants that he could wear both to the office and out on the town. I’m a big fan of the ones he chose. They have the tiniest bit of sheen and a little give, so they’re comfy while also looking sharp. He just bought two more pairs in blue and khaki. Thrive Causemetics Tubing Mascara Courtesy of Thrive Causemetics Shop Thrive SHOP AMAZON I decided to finally hop on the tubing mascara bandwagon, and Thrive’s was the one I saw most recommended on Reddit. items.descriptionOriginal: This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. Earlier this year, on a trip to Dominica to learn about the sperm whales that live in those Caribbean waters, Maya Higa was offered the chance to swim with them. She said no. Her reason was simple. “She would not participate in an activity that her followers would not be able to do,” wrote Maggie Kaplan, who nominated Maya for this series and was on the same trip. For most wildlife creators, that would have been the perfect moment for the cameras to come out. Maya turned on her livestream instead, talked with the boat crew and local staff about their work and lives, and shared the whales from her view on the surface. Kaplan came away moved by Maya’s resolve. “I was very impressed with her dedication on all fronts,” she wrote. But what she was describing wasn’t a sacrifice. It was consistency. Maya was doing exactly what she built Alveus Sanctuary to do. Building Alveus Maya founded Alveus in 2021 with a 21-hour charity stream on Twitch that raised more than $500,000. The platform came after the expertise, not the other way around. She grew up in Northern California and studied agricultural education and communication at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo. In college, she took a job as a zookeeper and completed internships at AZA-accredited facilities. She even got her falconry license. Part of the work involved going to schools and birthday parties to teach kids about animals in person, which gave her a taste for hands-on outreach and education. She went on to become a licensed wildlife rehabilitator. When she started streaming, all of that prior knowledge and experience came with her. Alveus is both a physical wildlife sanctuary in Austin, Texas, and a virtual education center. The sanctuary houses non-releasable animal ambassadors, animals that can’t survive in the wild but can represent their species and the ecosystems they come from. A 24/7 livestream on Twitch lets viewers watch them, get to know them by name, and connect with information about their wild counterparts. Other content creators can visit the sanctuary, run education programs, and extend the conservation message into communities Alveus wouldn’t otherwise reach. What exactly is Alveus? Alveus is both a physical wildlife sanctuary in Austin, Texas, and a virtual education center. The sanctuary houses non-releasable animal ambassadors, which are animals that can’t survive in the wild but can represent their species and the ecosystems they come from. A 24/7 livestream on Twitch lets viewers watch them, get to know them by name, and connect with information about their wild counterparts. Other content creators can visit the sanctuary, run education programs, and extend the conservation message into communities Alveus wouldn’t otherwise reach. Conservation for a generation that grew up on Twitch The demographic Maya is reaching is one that traditional conservation organizations have struggled with for years. Maya “is reaching a whole new generation of 18 to 30 year olds through social media platforms that speak to their demographic,” Kaplan wrote. That generation didn’t grow up watching nature documentaries on television. They watch streams, follow creators, and decide what they care about based on communities they already belong to. “She is creating a new type of outreach,” Kaplan wrote, “a teaching platform about different species and their importance to our environment.” A teaching platform built around the creator-viewer relationship works differently from a broadcast. Viewers are compelled to come back. They recognize the individual animals. They get into discussions in the chat about things they’ve learned. Conservation education needs that kind of sustained attention, and with conventional methods, it doesn’t get it very often. Maya has over a million followers across her platforms, and those followers have made Alveus financially self-sustaining through their donations. Twitch donated $100,000 to the sanctuary directly. A partnership with WWF extended the work beyond the sanctuary itself. And Maya’s own TED talk, “ The wildlife sanctuary you can visit from anywhere ,” which she delivered in London earlier this year, brought the model to an even broader professional audience. What comes next By 2026, Alveus has raised more than $7.5 million for conservation causes since its founding. The organization is actively expanding: new animal ambassadors coming in, enclosures being built out, and staff added to keep pace. Two projects are currently underway. The Pollinator Census is Alveus’s first community science initiative, where community members observe pollinator species in the sanctuary’s garden, and entomologists identify them, generating data to support insect conservation research. The larger effort is the Alveus Research and Recovery Institute (ARRI), developed in partnership with the Association of Zoos and Aquariums ‘ Saving Animals from Extinction (SAFE) program. ARRI’s first goal is a conservation breeding and release program for two critically endangered species: the Mexican Gray wolf and the Red wolf. It moves Alveus from education into direct intervention in species survival. The sperm whale moment in Dominica illustrates something about the whole operation. Maya went to Dominica to learn. When the choice came up, she ran the same calculation she’s always run: the point isn’t the experience she gets to have. It’s the one her audience gets to share with her. With a million people watching, that adds up to a different kind of reach than the field has seen. Learn more at bio.link/mayahiga . The post Maya Higa built a wildlife sanctuary on Twitch, funded by the people who watch it first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Two coral fragments fell over in a Stanford lab tank. When they touched, one healed the other. The bleached fragment, starved of the symbiotic algae that give coral both its color and its nutrition, began recovering within days. “We watched the healthy coral send over these colourful beneficial algae over to the bleached corals, and we watched its colour restore basically in front of our eyes,” said ocean scientist Danny Collins . Within a couple of weeks, the dying coral had recovered to the point where it was indistinguishable from its healthy neighbor. “We were blown away,” Collins said. “It does seem like this could open a door to possible reef restoration.” The findings , published last month in Science Advances , suggest that bleached coral is not necessarily dead, and that it can recover faster than researchers expected. The magic of the tissue bridge The recovery requires direct physical contact and a genetic match. When Collins’s team separated the fragments by a few millimeters, nothing happened. When they introduced corals from different genetic backgrounds, the corals rejected each other the way a body might reject a donated organ. When genetic clones made contact, their tissues fused. “They create a tissue bridge that kind of acts as a nutrient highway that allows for the healthy coral to then send over nutrients and this colourful algae over to the bleached coral,” Collins said. Coral is a colonial animal, a single organism made of thousands to millions of individual polyps. Fragments of the same genetic background recognize each other on contact and merge rather than fight. Collins noted this serves a natural function. If a piece breaks off in a wave, it can reconnect with the original colony. 96 percent of reefs are at risk The International Union for Conservation of Nature announced that about 96 percent of the world’s shallow-water reef systems are critically endangered and could disappear by 2075. Coral reefs support between a quarter and a third of all marine species, along with fisheries and coastal economies that hundreds of millions of people depend on. Coral scientist Julia Cole, who was not involved in the study, called the Stanford findings “a glimmer of light.” Cole chairs the Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences at the University of Michigan. She was enthusiastic but clear-eyed about scale. “If you think about the scale of reefs as kilometers, or in the case of the biggest reefs, thousands of kilometers … something that requires coral-to-coral contact, it would be a very meticulous and kind of overwhelming project,” she said. Collins’s team is working on extracting algae from healthy reefs, culturing it in labs, and deploying it to protect at-risk reefs ahead of expected bleaching events. “We hope in the near future we can have some interventions that actually could be field deployable and possibly scalable,” he said. The restoration work doesn’t address what’s warming the ocean in the first place. “We know how to solve the warming climate that’s causing these problems,” Cole said. “It comes back to getting serious about reducing greenhouse gas emissions, getting off of fossil fuels and transitioning to a clean-energy economy .” Source study: Science Advances – Rapid coral bleaching recovery via symbiont transfer from healthy corals Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: Dietary guidelines seem to run the gamut depending on where you live. In Japan, grain-based dishes are the main focus, while Greece promotes the Mediterranean diet and the U.S. emphasizes protein . So nutrition scientists from around the globe recently came together to develop a compendium of advice that’s adaptable across cultures (and takes the health of the planet into account). Enter: the International Food Guide Pyramid. The team compared national and regional dietary guidelines from the United States, Canada, Germany, Australia, China, the Netherlands, and the Nordic countries, in addition to analyzing more than 250 scientific publications, to pinpoint the shared fundamentals of healthy eating. As it turns out, they may be more universal than it often seems. “Despite what people often hear, there’s actually substantial agreement in nutrition science about the foundations of healthy eating,” study lead Karen Della Corte said in a news release. She added that a balanced diet will look different for each person, so the guidelines are designed to be adjusted to include local, affordable, and culturally appropriate foods. The new food pyramid focuses on plant foods, healthier sources of fat and protein, and high-quality carbohydrates. At the base — representing the foundation of a nourishing diet — are vegetables and fruit as well as whole and low-glycemic index grains. Above that are plant-based proteins like beans, nuts, and seeds, as well as plant-based oils. Next up are fish, poultry, eggs, and certain dairy products, and at the top, for use sparingly, are refined grains, red and processed meats, butter, chips, sugary drinks and snacks, and salt. A 2025 report from the EAT-Lancet commission called for similarly plant-forward international guidelines, suggesting they could prevent 15 million premature deaths per year and reduce environmental impacts like greenhouse gas emissions. “Our diet has to be not only for our own health but also for the health of our planet,” said David Jenkins of the University of Toronto, creator of the glycemic index. “Our science base has to be appropriately comprehensive to include that.” Karen Della Corte Corte offered the following advice for putting the pyramid’s principles into practice: Design your meal around the plant food you want to emphasize, first thinking about which vegetables, whole grains, beans, or lentils you could include. Opt for beans, peas, lentils, fish, poultry, or yogurt more frequently than red or processed meats, and don’t make meat the biggest part of any meal. Reach for snacks like nuts, seeds, fruit, or vegetables with hummus over less nutritious processed options. Choose whole-grain bread over refined white bread and whole-grain or high-fiber cereals rather than refined, puffed, flaked, or popped cereals. Use canola or olive oil in your cooking instead of animal fats like butter or tallow. Drink water instead of soda.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Endangered Animals Making a Comeback in 2027 Reading Time: 4 minutes Endangered Animals Making a Comeback in 2027 When you hear about endangered wildlife, it’s often another story of shrinking habitats, declining populations or species facing extinction. However, there is good news worth celebrating, too. Thanks to dedicated conservation efforts, some of the world’s most threatened animals are making remarkable comebacks. From mountain gorillas thriving in protected forests to bald eagles soaring across North America, you’ll find encouraging examples of how conservation can reverse population declines. Discover inspiring wildlife recovery stories that offer hope to endangered animals and show how your support for conservation can make a difference. 1. Mountain Gorillas Decades of habitat protection, veterinary care and anti-poaching initiatives have helped mountain gorilla populations grow to over 1,000 individuals , with multiple family groups. It’s a significant improvement for a species that once faced a much bleaker future. You’ll find these great apes in two isolated regions of Central and East Africa, where conservation teams work alongside local communities to protect the remaining habitat. The survival of this primate species extends beyond the gorillas themselves. Protecting large primates can also preserve entire ecosystems. While mountain gorillas remain endangered, their growing numbers demonstrate the value of long-term conservation. Expanding these efforts to other primate species may also protect smaller endangered species. 2. Bald Eagles Few wildlife recoveries are as impressive as that of the bald eagle. Once threatened by hunting, habitat destruction and the irresponsible use of the pesticide commonly known as DDT, America’s national bird has made an extraordinary species comeback. DDT led to poor-quality egg production, making successful breeding incredibly difficult for bald eagles. The ban on DDT, stronger legal protections and habitat conservation helped reverse decades of population decline. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the population in the lower 48 states increased from approximately 72,434 birds in 2009 to just over 316,000 birds , with 71,467 breeding pairs tracked between 2018 and 2019. Today, you’ll see bald eagles near rivers, lakes and coastlines across much of North America. Their remarkable recovery shows how environmental laws and sustained conservation efforts can give threatened wildlife a second chance. 3. Sea Turtles For sea turtles, the journey to adulthood begins with a dangerous dash from nest to ocean. Fortunately, conservation programs are giving more hatchlings a fighting chance through beach patrols, nest monitoring and community involvement. In the Philippines, conservationists have even recruited four-legged helpers. Project CURMA’s Paw Patrol uses specially trained dogs to sniff out buried turtle eggs , allowing volunteers to locate and protect nests from poachers and other threats. Efforts to reduce accidental catches in fishing nets, restore nesting beaches and limit artificial lighting along the coastlines are helping protect sea turtles at different stages of their lives. Some populations have shown encouraging improvements following decades of protection. While several sea turtle species remain endangered or critically endangered, initiatives like these show that creative conservation strategies can improve their chances of survival. When you participate in community initiatives, such as Paw Patrol, you increase the support that struggling species need to survive. 4. Tigers Tigers have lost much of their historical range to deforestation, human development and poaching. However, conservation efforts in parts of Asia are helping these magnificent predators reclaim lost ground. Wild tigers live across parts of Asia, where conservation efforts have helped some populations rebound after the global population fell to an estimated 3,200 in 2010. India offers one of the strongest examples, as it is now home to about 70% of the world’s wild tigers. Forest conservation has played a valuable part in this and other success stories. Sustainable forestry and other interventions have slowed global deforestation rates by almost 40% since the 1990s, which is why purchasing sustainably sourced timber is so important, whether you buy new floors, furniture or even musical instruments. Habitat loss remains a threat, but support for responsible forest management offers hope. 5. American Alligators American alligators were once hunted so extensively for their valuable skins that their survival became a serious concern. By 1967, the species had gained federal endangered status, prompting stronger protections against hunting and illegal trade. Conservation measures, including regulated harvesting and wetland management, helped restore their numbers. The species was removed from the U.S. endangered species list in 1987, just two decades after receiving protection. Today, up to 1.06 million mature American alligators inhabit the southeastern United States. With the species now classified as least concern, you’re looking at one of America’s most successful wildlife recovery stories. 6. Other Stories of Recovery The good news continues across the world. Other threatened species are showing encouraging signs of recovery, giving you even more reasons to feel hopeful about wildlife conservation. The Iberian lynx has rebounded from near extinction, thanks to captive breeding and habitat restoration across Spain and Portugal. North Atlantic right whales are also showing tentative signs of population growth, although their survival remains precarious. Meanwhile, giant pandas have benefited from decades of habitat protection and breeding programs, while southern white rhinos have recovered significantly from historical population lows through intensive conservation efforts. Humpback whales offer another success story, with several populations rebounding after commercial whaling restrictions gave these ocean giants a chance to recover. These achievements highlight the importance of patience and persistence, as rebuilding wildlife populations often requires decades of protection and ongoing monitoring. Every contribution makes a difference, and even keeping your distance from these animals, respecting protected habitats and choosing ethical wildlife tourism experiences contribute to various species’ success stories. Why Are More Endangered Animals Recovering? Wildlife recovery rarely happens by chance. Behind these success stories are years of coordinated conservation efforts, scientific research and communities working to protect vulnerable species. These efforts also benefit entire ecosystems. When you protect forests, wetlands and oceans, you’re helping preserve the habitats that countless species depend on for survival. Several approaches are helping endangered animals rebuild their populations: Habitat protection: National parks, wildlife corridors and sustainable land management give animals safer places to live, breed and find food. Stronger wildlife laws: Hunting restrictions, anti-poaching patrols and international trade regulations help reduce human-driven threats. Breeding and reintroduction programs: Conservationists can raise threatened animals in protected environments and then release them into suitable habitats where they have a better chance of thriving. Community involvement: Local conservation projects encourage people to protect wildlife while supporting livelihoods through responsible tourism and sustainable practices. Scientific monitoring: Tools like GPS collars, population surveys, and genetic research help conservationists spot problems earlier and celebrate progress when recovery efforts work. A Brighter Future for Endangered Wildlife Every species making a comeback represents years of dedication and a reminder that extinction isn’t always inevitable. Although many endangered animals still face serious threats, these conservation successes show that meaningful progress is possible. You can help sustain that momentum by supporting wildlife conservation organizations, choosing responsibly sourced products and spreading awareness about threatened species. Even small actions contribute to a broader movement to protect biodiversity. With continued commitment, today’s recovery stories could become tomorrow’s thriving wildlife populations. The post Endangered Animals Making a Comeback in 2027 appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A former Los Angeles gang member, a former skinhead and a former radical Islamist walk into a youth center. What sounds like the setup for an uneasy joke is at the core of Farah Pandith’s work: Put people who might otherwise never share a room in front of young people; let them explain what drew them into extremism and how they found their way out. “They’re the most authentic and credible voices there are,” Pandith says. More than once she has observed that their stories reach an audience that official warnings cannot. For decades, including while working for the U.S. government under the Obama, George W. Bush and George H.W. Bush administrations, Pandith researched why people embrace ideologies that divide the world into “us versus them.” Before people can be persuaded away from hatred, she argues, one has to understand what they are looking for: recognition, certainty or a place in the world. “You don’t suddenly explode and become an extremist overnight. You’re having some self-doubt, you’re asking questions about who you are,” she says from her light-filled living room in Arlington, Virginia. Preventing someone from becoming an extremist has been her lifelong goal, because it’s “infinitely easier than dealing with the fallout.” Farah Pandith visits the Indonesian city of Bekasi during her time as the U.S. special representative to Muslim communities. Credit: U.S. Embassy, Jakarta / Wikimedia Commons While working for the government, she traveled to nearly 100 countries, from Belgium to Bangladesh, to understand how extremists’ descent into violence can be interrupted. Today she applies what she learned to a broader problem: how to make compassion more than an admirable sentiment and help communities put it into practice. Last year Pandith received the ADL Daniel Pearl Award , which is given annually to a person who has had a positive impact on understanding between Jews and the Muslim world, and is sponsored by the parents of the journalist who was kidnapped and killed in Pakistan in 2002. “It is hard to think of anyone more knowledgeable than Farah Pandith when it comes to countering violent extremism,” Joseph Nye, the late chair of the National Intelligence Council, said about her. On September 11, 2001, Pandith watched on television like millions of others as two planes struck the World Trade Center. “It felt very heavy,” she recalls, putting a hand to her heart. “The world kind of went still for a moment, like, ‘What do we do about this?’” She felt compelled to act, to help prevent such violence from happening again. She especially rejected the way extremists attempted to define her religion on the airwaves. “Who are they to dictate what Islam is?” she remembers thinking. “For me, Islam means humility, compassion, to treat others with respect.” Initially, when she worked for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), cooperating with local organizations showed her that effective policy depends on understanding the people on the ground. “You have to listen really well to find a solution that matches with the local community,” she says. “That’s tricky and complex. Trust has to be built first.” The same principle, she realized, applied to preventing violent extremism. Government officials could not design effective strategies from Washington alone. They needed to hear from the people they hoped to reach, including those whose voices had been overlooked. After joining the National Security Council in 2004, Pandith helped develop the “soft power” side of the Global War on Terror through a new approach called Countering Violent Extremism. Military action might disrupt extremist organizations, but it could not prevent them from recruiting new members. Nor were public relations campaigns successful in overcoming the distrust of Muslims worldwide. Even in her own government, distrust was impossible to ignore. One congressman called the White House to complain a “jihadist” was sitting in the Council. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Pandith was briefly living in Afghanistan’s capital, Kabul, in 2004 when photographs of abuse at Abu Ghraib surfaced showing American soldiers humiliating Muslim prisoners. “In an instant, all our efforts on the ground were harmed irreparably,” she says. Locals asked how she could represent a government that treated Muslim prisoners that way. The experience reinforced a lesson: Building trust also meant receiving criticism, sitting through uncomfortable conversations. Pandith carried that approach into her work at the State Department, where Hillary Clinton appointed her the first U.S. special representative to Muslim communities in 2009. Instead of treating Muslim populations as a single audience for American messages, she traveled widely, meeting people in homes, mosques and community settings to learn what mattered to them. “You have to go to the rural areas,” she says, aiming to support credible local voices that could offer alternatives to extremist narratives. Pandith herself has been shaped by a background that made her an ideal diplomat. She came to the U.S. from Kashmir as a baby with her mother, a pulmonologist and the medical director of a hospital. Pandith describes growing up in a highly educated Muslim family without experiencing discrimination. She remembers an America in which people of different faiths could live alongside one another, “with a synagogue, a church, a mosque and a temple in the same part of town.” Today, she admits, that harmonious coexistence feels nearly impossible. Her parents separated when she was 10, and her mother raised Pandith and her brother on her own. One of her greatest influences was her uncle, a heart surgeon. “I’ve held the hearts of different people in my hands,” he would tell her. “Always remember: There is no difference between the heart of a Muslim, a Jew, a Hindu or a Christian.” Pandith feels she carries “many identities” — an American, a woman, a Muslim and a foreign policy professional, among others. While traveling as Special Representative to Muslim Communities in the Obama administration, she said she had a “superpower” when speaking with Muslims. When she told them she was born in Srinagar in Kashmir, India, the atmosphere often changed. “Suddenly I’m like a sister to them.” Farah Pandith on a panel at the Milken Institute Asia Summit. Courtesy of Farah Pandith Her ability to forge connections would become one of her greatest professional assets. By chance, Barbara Bush, the wife of President George H.W. Bush, visited Smith College during Farah’s senior year. She was so impressed by a speech Pandith gave as student body president that she helped her secure her job at USAID after graduation. That was how the young woman began traveling around the world. Pandith’s work challenged conventional explanations of radicalization. Poverty and lack of education, she argued, could not explain why people embraced violent ideologies. Some of the 9/11 terrorists were well educated. Pandith pointed to a different cause she observed in Muslim communities: deep identity crises among young people who struggled to find their place in a rapidly changing world. She thinks of a young woman in Denmark whose Imam told her she wasn’t a Muslim if she didn’t cover her head. Or Mubin Shaikh in Canada, who went to Pakistan and Syria as a 19-year-old to fight alongside the jihadists and who now teaches security politics at the University of Ottawa. Pandith has seen firsthand that dialogue can change minds. ““It’s less interesting for the media than an extremist’s video, but the conversations we had affected people.” Her initiatives have sought to make dialogue a shared responsibility. Against Violent Extremism became the world’s first and only network of former extremists, launched by the U.S. Department of State, the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and Google. The “Hours Against Hate” campaign encouraged teenagers to spend an hour doing something for someone different from themselves. Millions participated. Sisters Against Violent Extremism connected mothers concerned about their children’s vulnerability to extremist recruitment. In a citizen-dialogue program, Pandith traveled through Europe with other Muslim Americans to share experiences and listen to local concerns. People had the chance to meet someone they might otherwise see only through stereotypes and to develop a relationship that complicated those assumptions. In her book How We Win , recently reissued, Pandith remains stubbornly optimistic: The fight against extremism can be won. Preventing people from being drawn into extremist movements requires intervening early and bringing together the people who can reach them — not just government officials, but business leaders, teachers, local communities and influencers whose networks, knowledge and credibility government agencies lack. “The fight against violent extremism is not going to be won solely by the efforts of government,” she argues. “We need businesses to step up as never before, for the public interest as well as their own.” She insists that this work cannot be dismissed as idealism or do-goodery but is “a matter of national security” — as important as the hard power of military force. Pandith emphasizes that the underlying lessons can be relevant for many communities. The same dynamics of exclusion and dehumanization can fuel hostility toward religious minorities, LGBTQ+ people and Asian communities, among others. Still, she admits that the strategies for countering violent extremism never fully came to fruition, often mired in bureaucracy. “Congress provided just 0.0138 percent of funding compared to the funding for the military,” she calculates. “We know what we need to do. We spent 25 years researching and exchanging strategies. But we left the field to the extremists.” Pandith sees the reality as a call to action: “We cannot just wring our hands and keep saying things are bad and things are difficult and somebody else’s problem. We need everybody.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime She now works outside government to advance another part of this agenda, as senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations , teaching countering violent extremism at Georgetown University, and as a Global Peace Laureate for the Muhammad Ali Center. She has been developing the Muhammad Ali Index on compassion . For Pandith, compassion is the capacity to recognize another person’s humanity even amid disagreement, and to resist the impulse to turn differences into a reason for contempt. “There isn’t a faith on planet Earth that doesn’t have compassion in it. And even if you are not religious you understand what it means, right?” As part of the Muhammed Ali Index, more than 5,400 people in 12 American cities responded to the 2025 State of Compassion survey . Sixty-one percent said they felt compassion has declined in the last four years, but 43 percent were optimistic about the future of compassion in America. A second index, planned for 2027, will cover 20 U.S. cities and 12 cities around the world. The ambition is practical. Pandith hopes the data will help mayors, school leaders, faith groups and local organizations identify opportunities to build stronger connections and design efforts suited to their own communities. The point is not to prescribe a universal program, but to create a framework that can be adapted. “We want to see people taking inspiration from the data to actually do something over time so we can measure and see what takes place,” she says passionately, insisting that compassion can be trained: “Compassion is a muscle that can be exercised.” Yet the starting point is personal: “Self-compassion is essential.” Building the capacity for compassion, Pandith argues, begins with recognizing what is happening inside oneself. She is particularly interested in reaching young people early. “The world that they are growing up in is so polarized and so difficult and so different from the one that we have grown up in,” she says, “that they don’t have a memory of people who are different from them speaking to each other with dignity regularly.” As Pandith sees it, waiting for polarization to disappear on its own is not a strategy. The task is to build relationships and connections that open up hearts and minds — and to keep investing in them long enough to learn what works. She repeats her favorite sentence: “Solutions are available and affordable.” UPDATE — November 3, 2026: This story has been updated to clarify facts about Pandith’s work and background. items.descriptionOriginal: Some bees line their nests with soft petals. Some line them with hardened tree sap. Some line them with a thin, flexible film composed of silk and polyester. And this latter group—known as cellophane bees—may hold the key to sustainable, biodegradable plastic, according to a new study. “Nature has already solved a problem that polymer scientists are still working on: a bioplastic that is chemically and physically similar to conventional plastics but doesn’t persist in the environment,” says study team member Jonathan Coote , assistant professor in the Department of Sustainable Biomaterials at Virginia Tech University. Unlike more familiar hive-dwelling honeybees, cellophane bees nest in the soil. Females lay eggs in individual chambers that they line with secretions from a gland on their abdomen. Scientists have known for almost half a century that this lining is composed of silk fibers and a polyester similar to polyethylene—a material that makes up about one-third of human-produced plastics and is the most commonly used plastic for packaging. “Polyethylene-like polyesters made in the lab generally don’t break down well in the environment,” says Coote. “The bees’ material, however, breaks down rapidly in soil.” Although the bees nest in aggregations of 10,000 or more individual nests and often use the same nest sites for decades, their habitat never becomes choked with plastic—in contrast to large aggregations of modern humans. To find out more about how the bees do it, Coote and his collaborators gathered nest linings from two Tennessee nest sites of a species of cellophane bee known as Colletes inaequalis . They put the material through a battery of tests to characterize its structure and chemical makeup. They also collected nest linings that had been in the ground for four, seven, and 11 months to track how the material degrades over time. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby The tradeoff at the heart of bioplastics. A fresh nest cell lining is about 73% polyester and 27% silk by weight, the researchers report. The polyester is semicrystalline, likely has cross-linked polymer chains, and has a crystal structure and degradation temperature similar to that of polyethylene. “The biggest surprise was that the material is most likely cross-linked, meaning its polymer chains are chemically tied together into a network,” says Coote. “Cross-linked plastics, called thermosets, are typically very durable, and designing thermosets that break down at the end of their life is a major challenge in polymer science. So finding a thermoset that breaks down rapidly in soil was very counterintuitive, and it’s exciting to have a natural example to learn from.” By four months, the nest linings are just 40% polyester, meaning that the polyester degrades even more rapidly than famously biodegradable silk in the first months (after that, the composition changes much more slowly). Four-month-old nest linings remain flexible and intact, protecting the nest cell from moisture and microbes like a shrink-wrapped bell pepper at the grocery store. By seven months, about the time the larva has developed into an adult bee, the lining easily cracks easily; by 11 months, it crumbles in the hand. In other words, unlike that bell pepper’s shrink wrap, the nest lining lasts just as long as is needed to protect the developing bee, and no longer. The researchers next aim to investigate how the material breaks down so quickly. They hypothesize that the particularities of polyester’s crystal structure may leave the bonds that connect the material’s subunits exposed to a greater degree than in other polyesters. There’s also evidence of an enzyme that breaks these bonds present in the nest lining, perhaps from the mother bee’s saliva. “The goal is to reverse engineer what the bees are doing so that we can design similar materials in the lab and eventually produce them at practical scale,” Coote says. Source: Coote J.P., et al. “ Rapid soil degradation of a cross-linked, semicrystalline polyethylene-like polyester produced by Colletes bees .” PNAS 2026. Image: Laura Russo.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Wildlife Conservation Filmmaking Turns Powerful Stories into Real-World Action Reading Time: 3 minutes Wildlife conservation filmmaking connects audiences with wild places and the people protecting them. Wildlife conservation filmmaking gives viewers a reason to care about wild places they may never see in person. Fin and Fur Films , an award-winning production company, builds its work around that idea. Its team focuses on wildlife, adventure, and conservation stories. The company says it is proudest of films that led to real-world conservation impacts. That goal shapes every project. In wildlife conservation filmmaking, a film succeeds when it moves audiences to care, not just when it entertains. Ben Masters, founder and director, started the company in 2012 with a Kickstarter campaign. Kickstarter is an online fundraising platform where many people donate small amounts. That campaign paid for the film Unbranded. Unbranded follows four young cowboys who adopted, trained, and rode a string of wild mustangs 3,000 miles from Mexico to Canada. That is about the distance across the continental United States. The route crossed some of the wildest terrain in the American West. The trip included runaway horses, a sassy donkey, perilous mountain passes, and rodeos. It also brought sickness, injury, and death. The film won the Audience Award at Telluride Mountainfilm and the Hot Docs Film Festival. Unbranded also shines a light on the complex situation facing the country’s wild horses. The adventure holds attention, and the film explains the issue along the way. Wildlife conservation filmmaking often works this way. The River and the Wall takes a similar approach. Five friends travel 1,200 miles from El Paso to the Gulf of Mexico through the unknown wilds of the Texas borderlands. They go by horse, mountain bike, and canoe. That distance equals nearly a full day of nonstop highway driving, but the friends covered it much more slowly. They set out to document the borderlands. They also wanted to explore how a border wall could affect the natural environment. As the wilderness gave way to the more populated Lower Rio Grande Valley, the friends met the human side of the immigration debate. The trip took an emotional turn they had not planned for. Deep in the Heart: A Texas Wildlife Story brings wildlife conservation filmmaking to an entire state. Actor Matthew McConaughey narrates the visually stunning film. It celebrates Texas landscapes and wildlife found nowhere else. Wildlife conservation filmmaking comes to an entire state in Deep in the Heart: A Texas Wildlife Story , narrated by Matthew McConaughey, a visually stunning film celebrating Texas landscapes and wildlife found nowhere else. Photo courtesy of Fin and Fur Films . The film aims to protect the state’s remaining wild places. It shows how water and wildlife depend on each other. It also recognizes Texas’s important role in conservation across the continent. Reach matters in wildlife conservation filmmaking. Fin and Fur Films has shared its work through Netflix, Apple TV, PBS Nature, Prime, National Geographic, and LoveNature. The films have also appeared in large theatrical releases and on international television. Global Wildlife Conservation notes that well-made environmental documentaries can bring people closer to nature and inspire them to protect it. The Fin and Fur Films catalog shows how that works in practice. Each story pairs a real adventure with a real conservation question. Partnerships help wildlife conservation filmmaking go further. The company has worked with American Rivers, The Nature Conservancy, and Texan by Nature. It has also partnered with brands such as H-E-B and YETI. The numbers show how far a small team can stretch. The company has produced five feature films and more than 30 short films. It has worked with more than 40 conservation groups, which is roughly one partner group per film. See also: A Documentary About Overfishing Sparked Blue Marine Foundation’s Ocean Conservation Mission Masters says the crew keeps its roots as river lovers, backcountry horsemen, and field-savvy wildlife biologists. He also stresses that each film is a team effort. Dozens, or even hundreds, of people contribute to each one. Masters credits partners, collaborators, donors, contractors, and the viewers who give their time to watch. That shared support keeps the work going. Audiences are part of the effort, too. Good stories make conservation feel personal. Wildlife conservation filmmaking gives those stories a wide audience. Which wild place would you most like to see protected next? The post How Wildlife Conservation Filmmaking Turns Powerful Stories into Real-World Action appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Goldman Prize Honors Young Activist for Stopping Fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River Towns Reading Time: 3 minutes Yuvelis Morales Blanco won the 2026 Goldman Environmental Prize for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities and helping halt two pilot projects and secure a landmark court ruling. A university student began stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns by knocking on her neighbors’ doors. Seven years later, Yuvelis Morales Blanco has won the 2026 Goldman Environmental Prize for that work. The prize honors grassroots environmental leaders from six world regions each year. Her campaign helped stop two pilot fracking projects near her hometown of Puerto Wilches. It also led to a Constitutional Court ruling that upheld her Afro-Colombian community’s right to a say. To date, no fracking project has moved forward anywhere in Colombia. Morales Blanco, now 24, grew up in a family of subsistence fishers on the Magdalena River. The river flows nearly 1,000 miles from the Andes to the Caribbean, about the distance from Boston to Atlanta. For the roughly 30,000 people of Puerto Wilches, it provides food, income, and identity. The town also sits in the heart of Colombia’s oil country. Ecopetrol, the largest and majority state-owned oil company, is based in nearby Barrancabermeja. Between 2015 and 2022, about 40% of its more than 2,000 oil spills happened in this region. That works out to roughly two spills a week for eight years. In 2018, a leak at the Lizama 158 well displaced about 100 families and killed thousands of fish. So when the government proposed fracking nearby, residents had reason to worry. In 2019, then-President Iván Duque announced two pilot projects called Kalé and Platero. Ecopetrol led both, with ExxonMobil as operator and majority partner on Platero. Fracking, short for hydraulic fracturing, pumps water, sand, and chemicals into rock at high pressure. The pressure cracks the rock and frees trapped oil or gas. The process uses large amounts of water and can contaminate rivers and groundwater. Morales Blanco was studying environmental engineering at the time. She paused her degree and began visiting neighbors to explain the risks. She also joined the Alianza Colombia Libre de Fracking, or Colombia Free from Fracking Alliance. With the alliance, she helped lead protests outside the Ecopetrol refinery. In January 2022, she testified at permit hearings and organized a peaceful sit-in. Soon after the sit-in, armed men showed up at her home. She fled Colombia, and France granted her asylum in February 2022. No one has been convicted for the threats against her. Exile in France did not end her campaign. She received the Marianne Initiative award for human rights defenders and raised the issue with President Emmanuel Macron. She also brought the case before the International Rights of Nature Tribunal. Back home, the campaign for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns began winning in court. In April 2022, a court suspended environmental permits for both projects until companies consulted local communities. Months later, newly elected President Gustavo Petro announced his opposition to fracking. Community organizing helped secure a court-ordered suspension of two fracking projects in 2022, a key step in stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River, followed months later by President Gustavo Petro’s opposition to fracking. Photo by Christian Escobar Mora courtesy of Goldman Environmental Prize . Ecopetrol suspended the project contracts in September 2022. By November, it had halted Kalé and Platero and undone its agreements with ExxonMobil. The decisive ruling came in August 2024. Colombia’s Constitutional Court found that the pilots violated the community’s right to free, prior, and informed consent. Under this principle, companies must consult communities and win their agreement before projects affect their land. That decision reaches beyond Puerto Wilches. It confirms that Afro-Colombian communities have a legal voice over what happens on their territory. The precedent matters for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities and anywhere similar projects appear. Morales Blanco has since returned to Puerto Wilches and keeps organizing with the alliance. She describes the Magdalena as the life that sustains her family and her fishing community. She also points out that her region produces great energy wealth while many residents stay poor. The Global Greengrants Fund, which supports the alliance, notes that each prize winner represents a broader movement. More than 80 of the fund’s partners and allies have received the prize since 1993. Afro-Colombian fishing communities stood beside her in stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns. Morales Blanco won for the South and Central America region, one of six 2026 winners , all of whom were women. The others came from Nigeria, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Papua New Guinea, and the United States. Colombia’s politics have shifted since her win. President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August 2026 after campaigning to expand fracking. Still, the 2024 ruling gives communities like Puerto Wilches firm legal ground to demand a say. Stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities didn’t require a big budget or political office. It took a young woman who knew her river and kept going after threats forced her abroad. Her prize shows how local action can shape national policy. The post Goldman Prize Honors Young Activist for Stopping Fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River Towns appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Τετράγωνα αγάπης που ηρεμούσαν ένα παιδί
items.titleOriginal: Squares of Love that Calmed a Child
items.description: Ένα μικρό πλεκτό σωληνάκι —ανοιχτό και στις δύο άκρες, αρκετά φαρδύ για δύο χέρια — και ένα παιδί με άγχος βρέθηκαν σε μια αυστριακή τάξη. Αυτή η ήσυχη στιγμή βρίσκεται στο επίκεντρο του δεκαετούς έργου της Ursula Kermer, Mehr ist Mehr ("More is More"), ένα δίκτυο εθελοντών που μετατρέπει μεμονωμένα τετράγωνα νήματος σε κουβέρτες, μπολερό και κουβέρτες.…
items.descriptionOriginal: A small knitted tube — open at both ends, just wide enough for two hands — and a child with anxiety found each other in an Austrian classroom. That quiet moment is at the heart of Ursula Kermer's decade-long project, Mehr ist Mehr ("More is More"), a volunteer network that turns individual squares of yarn into blankets, boleros, and twiddle muffs for people moving through hard seasons of life. Kermer, an art therapist, is honest about what the project cannot do: "Our project does not solve problems; it does not make crisis go away." But it is constant, and that constancy — the weekly knitting circles, the puzzling together of mismatched squares, the packages of wool arriving unbidden from strangers — turns out to be its own kind of medicine. The blankets travel to families whose children have cancer, to people who cannot pay their heating bills, to rehabilitation centers where a counselor leaves them draped over chairs so that someone in crisis might simply reach out and choose one. Most knitters never know whose hands will eventually hold their work, and Kermer photographs every step so they know where it ends — just not with whom. She describes the whole endeavor as resilience training in disguise: choosing a color, trusting a process, watching mismatched pieces become something whole. For her, the image that holds it all is a network — "growing and moving, and provides a resilient safety" — as easily overlooked, but just as strong as the individual threads that compose spools of yarn.
